James Blunt collected the Icon Award, joking that he has gone from being labelled a one-hit wonder to becoming 'just an internet meme', and delivered one of the night's most entertaining speeches as he accepted the prize, presented in connection with Visit West Hollywood. Blunt, who recently fulfilled a tongue-in-cheek promise to adopt the name Ryan Bel Air after Airplane Mode reached number one, has enjoyed a career spanning more than two decades behind global hits including 'You're Beautiful'. Wolf Alice collected the Group Award, with vocalist Ellie Rowsell taking the trophy from Fearne Cotton, rounding out a strong year for the north London band. Blossoms won the Live Act Award, collecting the prize days before their first arena tour behind their sixth album, Songs from the Wedding Cake. Holly Humberstone won Song of the Year for 'To Love Somebody', taken from her 2026 album Cruel World. The Album Award went to HELP(2), the multi-artist War Child charity set featuring Fontaines D.C., Arctic Monkeys, Wolf Alice, The Last Dinner Party and others. British rap pioneer Giggs received the Trailblazer Award, Rachel Chinouriri was named Artist of the Year, and Saturday Night Live UK took the Television Award. Emerging talent was recognized too, with Madra Salach collecting the Breakthrough Award, Arjé Rayne receiving the Untapped Award and kwn crowned the Play Next winner. Hosted by Danny Dyer for a second consecutive year, the ceremony featured performances from Shygirl, Madra Salach and Arjé Rayne, while Jacob Lusk delivered a tribute to Freddie Mercury and George Michael.

articles.title: YouTube rejects the UK government's request to take down a Russell Brand video
articles.description: YouTube has rejected a request from the UK government to remove a video by Russell Brand, Rolling Stone reports. The refusal sets up a fresh clash between the platform and British authorities over how much power governments should have to order content removed. Brand remains a polarizing figure whose videos continue to draw large audiences despite the serious allegations against him.
articles.body: YouTube has rejected a request from the UK government to take down a video by Russell Brand, according to Rolling Stone. The decision puts the platform on a collision course with British authorities at a moment when governments in the UK and Europe are pressing tech companies to act faster on harmful and misleading content. Brand, the comedian and commentator, has remained a high-profile and polarizing figure online, and his videos continue to draw large audiences even as he faces serious allegations. YouTube's refusal to comply with the takedown request raises familiar questions about where the line sits between government pressure and platform independence, and about how consistently the company applies its own rules when the request comes from a state rather than from its own moderation systems. The UK government has been pushing platforms to take more responsibility for what circulates on their services, and a public refusal from YouTube is likely to feed into the wider debate over online safety law and enforcement. For creators and publishers, the episode is a reminder that takedown requests from governments do not automatically succeed, and that the biggest platforms are willing to push back when they judge a request to go beyond their policies.

articles.title: Mariah Carey's big Christmas hit gets released on tiny vinyl
articles.description: Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' is getting a tiny vinyl release, Rolling Stone reports, as the song begins its annual climb back up the charts. The novelty format is the latest way the 1994 classic keeps finding new audiences and new revenue three decades on. This week the track is already back at No. 18 on the Hot 100, with Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' at No. 14.
articles.body: Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' is getting released on tiny vinyl, Rolling Stone reports, as the 1994 classic begins its annual return to the charts. The miniature format is the latest novelty twist for a song that has become one of the most durable commercial assets in pop music, generating fresh sales and streams every holiday season more than three decades after its release. The timing is no accident: the Christmas chart season is already under way, with Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' at No. 14 on this week's Hot 100 and Carey's own hit back at No. 18, alongside a wave of seasonal re-entries including Bobby Helms' 'Jingle Bell Rock' and Brenda Lee's 'Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree'. Carey's song has now logged 22 weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 across its lifetime, a record for a holiday song, and its yearly return has become a fixture of the music calendar. Small-format and collectible vinyl has become a growth niche for labels looking to sell physical product to fans who already stream everything, and a miniature pressing of the most famous Christmas song of the modern era is an obvious fit. For Carey, whose holiday branding now spans the whole season, the tiny vinyl is one more way the song keeps earning long after most hits fade.

articles.title: Snoh Aalegra turned heartbreak into an LP with help from Stevie Wonder, Janet Jackson and more
articles.description: Snoh Aalegra has a new album shaped by heartbreak and built with an extraordinary cast of collaborators, including Stevie Wonder and Janet Jackson. Rolling Stone reports on how the Swedish-Iranian singer turned a painful period into a record, leaning on the guidance of artists she grew up admiring. The album continues her run as one of R&B's most refined voices.
articles.body: Snoh Aalegra has turned heartbreak into a new LP, and Rolling Stone reports that she made it with help from an extraordinary cast of collaborators, including Stevie Wonder and Janet Jackson. The Swedish-Iranian singer has built her reputation on refined, classicist R&B, and the new album draws directly on a painful personal period, reframing it through songs shaped with the guidance of artists she grew up admiring. Wonder's involvement brings one of the great songwriters of the last half-century into the room, while Jackson's presence connects the record to the lineage of pop and R&B royalty that has always informed Aalegra's sound. The piece traces how Aalegra worked through the material, leaning on collaboration rather than isolation to process the heartbreak at the record's center. For an artist whose previous albums earned her a devoted following and critical acclaim without chasing chart trends, the new LP is a statement of intent: a deeply personal record made with the help of legends. It also arrives at a moment when R&B's veteran voices are increasingly visible as mentors and collaborators for a younger generation, and Aalegra's album is one of the clearest examples of that exchange working on record.

articles.title: Pierce Brosnan welcomes Robert Pattinson into the James Bond role: 'Enjoy the ride'
articles.description: Former James Bond Pierce Brosnan has welcomed Robert Pattinson into the 007 role, telling him to 'enjoy the ride'. The passing of the torch between two Bonds comes as Amazon's Jeff Bezos confirmed he was personally involved in choosing Pattinson to play the spy. Brosnan played Bond in four films from 1995 to 2002.
articles.body: Pierce Brosnan has welcomed Robert Pattinson into the role of James Bond, telling the new 007 to 'enjoy the ride'. The message from one former Bond to the next is a classic piece of franchise ritual, and it lands as the casting of Pattinson continues to dominate film news. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said this week that he personally helped choose Pattinson for the role, telling reporters there was 'something special about Rob' after the Amazon chief was closely involved in the casting process. Brosnan played Bond in four films, from GoldenEye in 1995 through Die Another Day in 2002, and his blessing carries weight with fans who still regard his era fondly. Pattinson, best known for Twilight, The Batman and a run of acclaimed arthouse roles, is a less conventional choice than some of the names floated for the part, and the casting has split opinion among Bond watchers. Brosnan's warm welcome is the kind of public endorsement that helps settle a new Bond in with the audience, following a tradition in which outgoing 007s publicly embrace their successors. With Amazon now steering the franchise, the Pattinson era is shaping up as the biggest test yet of Bond's future.

articles.title: Meet the 'GTA' fans spending thousands on the setups they wanted as kids
articles.description: For the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, some fans are spending thousands of dollars on the gaming setups they dreamed about as kids, Rolling Stone reports. After 13 years waiting for a new GTA, players are marking the moment with high-end consoles, monitors and full battlestations. It is a sign of how much the game means to a generation that grew up with the series.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI finally launched on November 19 after 13 years of waiting, and Rolling Stone reports that some fans are marking the occasion by spending thousands of dollars on the gaming setups they wanted as kids. For players who grew up with the series, the new game is not just a release but a milestone, and the launch has become an excuse to build the dream battlestation: high-end consoles, big monitors, new chairs, lighting and audio, all assembled for the return to Vice City. The piece captures a generation of players who first encountered GTA as teenagers, sometimes on a shared family television, and who now have the money to buy the setup they imagined back then. It is also a snapshot of the game's scale as a commercial event: GTA VI has already banked more than $1.5 billion before launch and drew a record 20 million pre-orders, and the hardware spending around it shows how the launch ripples beyond software sales. Retailers and console makers have been leaning into the moment, and the fans profiled treat the setup as part of the experience rather than an accessory to it. For Rockstar, the enthusiasm is the payoff for more than a decade of anticipation, and for players it is a chance to finally play the game the way they always pictured it.

articles.title: P1Harmony scores first Billboard No. 1 as 'BLOW UP' tops the Top Album Sales chart
articles.description: P1Harmony has earned the first No. 1 of its career on a Billboard chart, with mini album BLOW UP debuting atop the Top Album Sales ranking dated November 21. The six-member group sold about 43,000 copies in the US in the week ending November 12, after previous releases peaked at No. 2 on the sales chart. The album also debuts at No. 4 on the Billboard 200, matching the group's best-ever position.
articles.body: South Korean group P1Harmony has secured the first No. 1 position of its career on a Billboard chart, with its latest mini album BLOW UP debuting at the top of the Top Album Sales ranking dated November 21, Billboard reported on November 20. According to Luminate, BLOW UP sold approximately 43,000 copies in the United States during the tracking week ending November 12, making it the best-selling album of the week in pure sales. The achievement marks a new milestone for the six-member act, whose previous releases had reached as high as No. 2 on the sales chart. It is also the group's seventh top-10 entry on Top Album Sales. BLOW UP, the group's tenth mini album, arrived on November 6 and set a new first-week sales record for P1Harmony in South Korea. The album also debuts at No. 4 on the Billboard 200, matching the group's previous best position on the all-genre chart, set by UNIQUE in March. Its 45,000 equivalent album units were built almost entirely on sales, with 43,500 of them from album purchases and only about 1,500 from streaming, a sales-first profile powered by 25 CD variants and five vinyl variants full of photocards and posters. Elsewhere on the Top Album Sales top 10, Kings of Leon and Steven Wilson debut, while Vince Guaraldi Trio's A Charlie Brown Christmas soundtrack returns and Ariana Grande's Christmas & Chill reaches the top 10 for the first time after a new vinyl variant. The result underlines how K-pop acts continue to convert physical fandom into US chart success.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo holds off Lil Baby for a fifth week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — by just 3,000 units
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo's 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love' spends a fifth nonconsecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 dated November 21, edging Lil Baby's FRESH by only 3,000 equivalent album units. Rodrigo earned 62,000 units to Lil Baby's 59,000 in one of the closest chart races of the season. The five weeks tie her debut album Sour for her longest run at No. 1.
articles.body: Olivia Rodrigo's you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love notches a fifth nonconsecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart dated November 21, 2026, holding off major new releases from Lil Baby and P1Harmony in one of the closest chart races of the season. In the tracking week ending November 12, Rodrigo's album earned 62,000 equivalent album units in the United States, up 9% according to Luminate data reported by Billboard. Lil Baby's FRESH debuted at No. 2 with 59,000 units, just 3,000 behind, in a contest decided by the balance between streaming and sales. Lil Baby actually out-streamed Rodrigo, pulling 56.81 million on-demand streams to debut at No. 1 on Top Streaming Albums, but he sold only 4,000 albums to her 11,000, and sales put her over the top. Rodrigo's album sales jumped 53% on the week, lifting it from No. 11 to No. 5 on Top Album Sales. The five weeks at No. 1 tie 2021's Sour for Rodrigo's longest command of the chart, and among albums released in 2026 no one has spent longer at the top, passing Drake's four weeks with ICEMAN. FRESH, announced October 20 and released November 6, is Lil Baby's eighth top 10 album, and remarkably all eight have debuted inside the top five. Morgan Wallen's I'm the Problem holds at No. 3 with 50,000 units, while P1Harmony's BLOW UP enters at No. 4 with 45,000 units and Ella Langley's Dandelion slips to No. 5 on the same total. FRESH also gives Lil Baby his fifth No. 1 on the Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, and its single 'Dead Fresh' reaches No. 1 on Hot Rap Songs. A sixth week at No. 1 would make Rodrigo's third album her biggest by that measure.

articles.title: Kings of Leon debut at No. 4 on Billboard's Top Rock chart with self-produced 'O My Beloved'
articles.description: Kings of Leon's tenth studio album, O My Beloved, debuts at No. 4 on Billboard's Top Rock & Alternative Albums chart dated November 21, the highest debut on the ranking this week. The album also becomes the band's sixth top-20 title on the Billboard 200. It is the first Kings of Leon record produced entirely by the four Followill brothers themselves.
articles.body: Kings of Leon will debut at No. 4 on Billboard's Top Rock & Alternative Albums chart dated November 21, 2026, with O My Beloved, the highest debut on the genre ranking this week. The placement also brings the band its sixth top-20 title on the Billboard 200. O My Beloved is the band's tenth studio album, released through Love Tap Records, and it marks the first time the four Followills, Caleb, Nathan, Jared and Matthew, have produced an entire studio album themselves. The album sold 11,000 copies in its first week, enough for a No. 6 debut on the Top Album Sales chart, and its arrival continues a chart career that has already produced No. 1 albums with Because of the Times, Only By The Night, Come Around Sundown, Walls and When You See Yourself. The record's writing centers on family, reflection and gratitude, according to the band, and the self-produced approach is a deliberate statement from a group more than two decades into its career. The debut shows the band's US audience is still there even as rock's chart presence has thinned, and it gives the Followills a new commercial marker to go with a record they made entirely on their own terms.

articles.title: Dominic Fike's 2018 song 'Babydoll' becomes his second Alternative Airplay No. 1 after a TikTok revival
articles.description: Dominic Fike's 'Babydoll', released in 2018 on a largely anonymous mixtape, has climbed to No. 1 on Billboard's Alternative Airplay chart after a resurgence driven in part by TikTok. It is Fike's second No. 1 on the chart and his first since '3 Nights' in 2019. The eight-year-old song's second life is the latest example of TikTok rewriting chart history.
articles.body: Dominic Fike's 'Babydoll', released in 2018, has become the singer's second No. 1 on Billboard's Alternative Airplay chart, according to Billboard's chart highlights for the week dated November 21. The song's rise is a revival story: it first appeared on a largely anonymous mixtape eight years ago and has found a second life this year thanks in part to TikTok, where the track has been picked up by a new wave of listeners. It is Fike's first chart-topper on the Alternative Airplay ranking since '3 Nights' in 2019. The result is the latest in a long line of TikTok-driven resurrections, in which songs years removed from their release return to the charts on the strength of short-form video. Billboard's own chart data underlines the platform's power: TikTok says 94% of songs that entered the Billboard Global 200 in 2025 went viral on its platform first. For Fike, the No. 1 gives an old song a new commercial life and a new audience, and it shows that a track's chart story no longer ends in its release year. The song's climb also reflects how alternative radio has become receptive to catalog tracks that arrive with proven streaming momentum.

articles.title: ENHYPEN to close out 'The Sin' series with spinoff album 'The Sin: Parallel World' on Friday
articles.description: ENHYPEN will release a three-track spinoff album, 'The Sin: Parallel World', on Friday, closing out their 'Sin' series. It is the group's third new release this year, following the EPs 'The Sin: Vanish' and 'The Sin: Bliss', which each sold more than 2 million copies in their first week. ENHYPEN also just dropped the new single 'I Want You' to close the series.
articles.body: ENHYPEN will roll out a three-track spinoff album, 'The Sin: Parallel World', on Friday, according to Belift Lab, bringing the group's 'Sin' series to a close. The forthcoming single album is the third new work the group is putting out this year, following seventh EP 'The Sin: Vanish' and eighth EP 'The Sin: Bliss'. Both mini albums sold over 2 million copies in their first week, and each entered the Billboard 200, at No. 2 and No. 1 respectively. The new release will be the final installment of the 'Sin' series, which has anchored ENHYPEN's 2026. The group also just dropped the new single 'I Want You' to close out the series, as reported by Billboard. ENHYPEN remains one of K-pop's most reliable chart acts, and the rapid cadence of three releases in a single year shows how the group's label is keeping the momentum going between full album cycles. For fans, the spinoff is a short, focused coda to a year-long storyline, and for the charts it is another release likely to make an immediate impact on the Billboard 200 and World Albums rankings.

articles.title: Michael Bublé's 'Christmas' vaults 119–35 on the Billboard 200 as the holiday season takes over the charts
articles.description: Michael Bublé's 2011 album Christmas vaults from No. 119 to No. 35 on the Billboard 200 dated November 21, the highest-charting seasonal album of the week. The jump leads a holiday takeover that also puts eight Christmas songs on the Hot 100, led by Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' at No. 14. The seasonal surge arrives earlier and stronger each year.
articles.body: Michael Bublé's Christmas, from 2011, vaults 119–35 on the Billboard 200 dated November 21, making it the highest-charting seasonal album of the week, according to Billboard's chart highlights. The leap of 84 places is the clearest sign yet that the holiday season has taken over the charts, with the album's annual return now a reliable fixture of the November rankings. The surge mirrors the Hot 100, where eight Christmas songs now chart, led by Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' at No. 14, up from No. 37, and Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' at No. 18, up from No. 39. Bobby Helms' 'Jingle Bell Rock' re-enters at No. 28, Brenda Lee's 'Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree' is back at No. 30, and Olivia Rodrigo's first holiday song, 'Take Me Home (4 Christmas)', debuts at No. 32. Ariana Grande's 'Santa Tell Me', Kelly Clarkson's 'Underneath the Tree' and Andy Williams' 'It's the Most Wonderful Time of the Year' are also back on the chart. Bublé's Christmas has become the definitive modern holiday album, returning to the top 40 every year without any new promotion, and its jump this week shows the seasonal catalog business at full strength. For labels, the holiday surge is now one of the most predictable revenue events of the year, and it arrives earlier each season.

articles.title: Jesse Eisenberg Can't Help Overthinking It
articles.author: Rachel Syme
articles.description: A warm, funny, 30-minute profile of the actor-director at his most neurotically self-aware — on his new film 'The Debut', the kidney he gave to a stranger, and why he can't stop overthinking everything.
articles.body:
Rachel Syme's profile of Jesse Eisenberg opens with the man himself: hyperverbal, relentlessly self-deprecating and visibly anxious, often to the point where his whole body shakes, 'like a dachshund in a thunderstorm'. Eisenberg, 43, has directed three feature films, all character studies of quirky, neurotic people whose lives look unremarkable from the outside. The film becomes a vehicle for his preoccupations with ego versus self-effacement, anxiety and OCD, and therapy — and Syme traces his career from 'The Social Network', including his decision to turn down its sequel, 'The Social Reckoning', to his current work. The new one is 'The Debut', out next month, which stars Julianne Moore as Mona Friedman, a meek middle-aged housewife in 1990s New Jersey who gets a part in a dumb musical and treats it like 'Raging Bull' — and becomes an egomaniacal actress in the process. Eisenberg wrote all thirteen songs in the show-within-the-film himself.

The profile follows Eisenberg through the strange double life he has built: a movie star since his teens, Oscar-nominated at 27 for playing Mark Zuckerberg in 'The Social Network', who insists — frantically — that he is not a typical famous person. He has written 25 humour pieces for The New Yorker, published a story collection, 'Bream Gives Me Hiccups', and built a career as a playwright, but says nobody in the film business cared about any of that until Emma Stone, his friend since 'Zombieland', backed his directing. His second film, 'A Real Pain', won Kieran Culkin an Oscar.

The piece's most striking material is about Eisenberg's urge to offset the advantages of fame. He and his wife, Anna Strout — a non-profit organiser and New York City public-school teacher whose family Syme describes as 'Marxist activists' — volunteer at Middle Way House, the domestic-violence shelter her mother built in Bloomington in the 1970s. He went on 'Millionaire' with Paul Giamatti, won half a million dollars and gave his half to the shelter. And last December he gave one of his kidneys to a stranger at NYU Langone, an idea he got a decade earlier from a podcast about altruistic organ donation. Syme's portrait is of a man whose anxiety and whose generosity are the same impulse: he pays obsessive attention to other people because he cannot stand small talk, and he keeps score against himself because fame feels unearned.

articles.title: Would You Dissect a Human Body?
articles.author: Dhruv Khullar
articles.description: A physician visits a lab where yoga teachers and massage therapists — not medical students — cut into cadavers, and asks what the rest of us can learn from holding a human body in our hands.
articles.body:
Dhruv Khullar, a practising physician and New Yorker writer, visits the Institute for Anatomical Research, a lab where the people cutting into donated cadavers are not medical students but yoga teachers and massage therapists — practitioners whose work depends on understanding the body from the outside, and who have decided they need to see it from the inside. The teacher behind the lab is Gil Hedley, who wants to 'democratize knowledge of the body'. The piece opens with one of his students, Sundip Aujla, a London-based alternative-medicine practitioner with a long grey beard who has trained in osteopathy, psychotherapy, Pilates and clinical hypnotherapy over a thirteen-year career — and whose life was changed by Hedley's 'Integral Anatomy' dissection videos. As a teenager, Aujla was better acquainted with delinquency, once taking refuge from a gang of young men with knives.

Khullar's question is what draws people like Aujla to the dissection table, and what they take away from it. For doctors, cadaver dissection is a rite of passage, a first encounter with mortality that is also a lesson in detachment. For the lay practitioners in this lab, it is something else: a chance to ground years of hands-on work in the actual architecture of muscle, fascia and bone — to feel the structures they have only imagined through skin. The piece explores the strange intimacy of the work, the ethics of who gets access to the dead, and the way a body on a table changes how you think about the living bodies you treat. It is a quiet, curious piece about expertise: how much of what we call knowing is really touching, and what happens when people who were never supposed to hold a scalpel pick one up.

articles.title: Big Oil, Climate Change, and a 'Smoking Gun'
articles.author: Rebecca John
articles.description: A major investigation, in collaboration with DeSmog, into the documents showing Shell funded climate science for decades while funding denial — and the typhoon survivors now suing the company in London.
articles.body:
Rebecca John's investigation, published in collaboration with DeSmog, opens with Arnold Obguia, who did not leave his island when Typhoon Rai — known locally as Odette — approached the Philippines in December 2021. The forecast said it was no big deal, just another tropical storm. A few hours later the winds escalated to 121 miles per hour sustained, with gusts of up to 167, and waves so large they almost pulled him out to sea. Clinging to a piece of broken sea wall, he survived; his house was completely destroyed. Now Arnold and more than 100 other survivors of the typhoon are suing Shell in the English courts, alleging the company helped make the typhoon more destructive through its contribution to historic greenhouse gas emissions and its funding of climate denial — despite knowing since at least 1965 that burning fossil fuels was the primary cause of man-made climate change.

The investigation's centre is a set of documents preserved at the University of East Anglia, rescued from a dumpster where they had been thrown after the retirement of the Climatic Research Unit's first director, the pioneering climatologist Hubert Lamb. They show Shell playing a pivotal role in establishing the unit — the UK's first specialist climate research centre, opened in 1972 — with an initial contribution of £10,000, later increased to £20,000, and then paying the unit to carry out an in-depth 'North Sea Storms Study' from the mid-1970s. The study warned that storm frequency was likely increasing because of CO2 — evidence one expert calls a 'smoking gun', since it shows the company funding research into the very risks it would later spend decades denying. Shell executive R. O. Chalkley first contacted Lamb in September 1966 after reading his work on climatic variability. In other words, the company was funding serious climate science — including research into worsening storms — at the same time as it would later fund campaigns denying the science. The case, taken up by the British law firm Hausfeld, was filed in full in July, and a date for the first hearing at London's High Court is expected early next year. Shell has dismissed the lawsuit as 'baseless', saying the company had no 'unique knowledge about climate change' and that it does not believe litigation is the right response, and it did not respond to a request for comment about its historical climate research. If the survivors win, the case could open the door for other hard-hit communities around the world to sue fossil-fuel companies on their home turf.

articles.title: Is Air Travel Getting Less Safe?
articles.author: James Fallows
articles.description: A veteran pilot investigates whether America's aviation system — long the safest in the world — is quietly fracturing, just as a week of outages and a nationwide ground stop put the question on everyone's mind.
articles.body:
James Fallows, a veteran pilot and longtime aviation writer, argues that the US aviation safety system — which went nearly sixteen years without a major-airline fatal crash until the January 29, 2025 collision over the Potomac that killed 67 people — is now under enormous strain from understaffing, overcrowding and deregulation. His question is whether the safest system in the world is quietly fracturing.

Fallows traces the 'lessons written in blood' behind that safety record: the 1956 Grand Canyon collision and the 2009 Buffalo crash each produced reforms — new rules, new technology, new institutions — that made the next disaster less likely. He contrasts that history with the present, in which the Trump administration has dismantled advisory committees, fired FAA staff, and failed to implement a third of the NTSB's 33 recommendations issued after the Potomac collision. The numbers point the same way: serious runway incursions rose from 7 in 2024 to 14 in 2025, with 2026 on a similar path.

Fallows writes from inside the cockpit culture — the checklists, the discipline, the habit of treating every small failure as a warning — and his argument is that safety in aviation is not a single thing but a system, and systems fail the way they did this week: not all at once, but in a cascade of small breakdowns that suddenly add up. He is careful to say that flying remains statistically very safe. The piece is a warning, not an alarm: the record was built deliberately, and it can be dismantled just as deliberately.

articles.title: Beto O'Rourke Says He'd 'Do Anything' for James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa — Including Work for Them
articles.author: Joe Hagan
articles.description: After the Democrats' shock victories in Texas, a portrait of Beto O'Rourke's second act: the twice-defeated candidate quietly building the party's future from behind the scenes.
articles.body:
After the Democrats' 2026 midterm victories in Texas — James Talarico flipping a Senate seat against Ken Paxton and Gina Hinojosa winning the governor's race — it was hard not to look over the shoulders of the two winners and see the shadow of Beto O'Rourke, Joe Hagan writes. O'Rourke, who lost statewide races for Senate in 2018 and governor in 2022, stepped aside a year ago, concluding the moment needed 'something and someone new', and threw himself into organising through his voter-registration group Powered by People.

Hagan's piece is a portrait of a politician in his second act. O'Rourke convened Talarico, Colin Allred and Joaquin Castro about a statewide slate, endured Paxton's attempt to prosecute his PAC, and criticised Chuck Schumer as Senate leader. He says he would do anything for Talarico and Hinojosa, including working in their administrations, and he is focused on winning Texas's 40 electoral votes in 2028. The piece asks what that shift means for the Democratic Party in Texas, a state Democrats have dreamed of flipping for a generation and where last week's results finally gave them something real to build on — and what it means for O'Rourke himself, whether a man who was once the future of the party can be content being its scaffolding.

articles.title: The EPA's Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn't Doing Its Job Anymore
articles.author: Ames Alexander
articles.description: A short, sharp investigation into a federal plane built to sniff out toxic disasters — now flying fewer missions and unable to give responders real-time data, just as chemical emergencies multiply.
articles.body:
The Environmental Protection Agency owns a plane with a very specific job: fly to the scene of a toxic disaster, sniff the air, and tell emergency responders in real time what chemicals they are dealing with. Ames Alexander reports that the EPA's ASPECT chemical-sensing Cessna isn't doing its job anymore. Designed to respond around the clock to toxic emergencies, it has answered only seven emergencies since early 2021 — and it stayed on the ground during an ammonia leak in Weatherford, Oklahoma, a Valero refinery fire in Texas, and a fatal recycling-plant explosion in Toledo.

In June the EPA's inspector general found the plane could no longer identify airborne chemicals in real time, with manual analysis taking about a week — too slow to guide evacuations. Former staff trace the decline to lost personnel and institutional knowledge since 2019. The EPA blames ageing sensors and expects replacements by 2027, but five former programme staff say the new sensors are the wrong fix — a concern underscored by disputed ASPECT data after the Smitty's Supply explosion and the East Palestine derailment.

The piece is a case study in how quiet, technical capabilities erode. The plane was built for the moments when minutes matter — a train derailment, a factory fire, a chemical spill — when first responders need to know what is in the air before they send people in. Now the aircraft sits idle more often, its missions cut back, its data delayed. For anyone who has watched a chemical fire on the news and wondered how the people on the ground know what they are breathing, the answer is increasingly that they don't — or not fast enough.

articles.title: Trump, Xi and Putin end first-ever trilateral summit with a four-point 'peace declaration' — but no Ukraine deal
articles.description: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin concluded their first-ever trilateral summit in Shenzhen on Thursday with a four-point joint declaration pledging UN reform, more refined petroleum supplies, limits on the International Criminal Court's jurisdiction and dialogue on reducing nuclear risks. The declaration does not mention Ukraine, a ceasefire or any nuclear arms limits, and sets no timetable — the historic format produced a statement of intent, not a breakthrough.
articles.body: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin concluded their first-ever formal trilateral summit on Thursday, November 19, in Shenzhen, China, with a four-point joint declaration titled the 'China-Russia-U.S. Heads of State Declaration toward Peace.' The roughly 80-to-90-minute meeting at Kylin Villa, held on the sidelines of the APEC summit, began nearly two hours late and ended without a joint press conference. The declaration reaffirms that 'a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,' commits the three countries to dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation, pledges to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products, calls for reform of the United Nations Security Council and states the International Criminal Court must not abuse its jurisdiction. It contains no numerical warhead limits, no verification mechanism, no implementation deadlines and no mention of Ukraine, Iran or a ceasefire — despite Ukraine being discussed in the leaders' remarks and in a separate 40-minute Trump-Putin meeting beforehand. Before the trilateral session, Trump and Xi also agreed to extend their trade truce, according to the Globe and Mail, CNBC and Bloomberg, though neither side said for how long or on what terms. The last US-Russia nuclear arms treaty, New START, expired in February 2026, and the three powers hold an estimated 5,042 (US), 5,420 (Russia) and 620 (China) warheads. Trump left Shenzhen for Washington soon after the talks without speaking to reporters.

articles.title: Satellite images show a collapsed span of the Crimean Bridge after Ukraine's third strike in a week
articles.description: Satellite images taken on Thursday show a collapsed span of the Crimean Bridge lying in the water after Ukraine's third attack on the crossing in a week. The road deck is visibly damaged and the parallel railway line is also hit, though rail traffic was reopened on Thursday after a temporary closure; the bridge remains closed to cars.
articles.body: Satellite images published on Thursday, November 19, show a collapsed span of the Crimean Bridge lying in the water after Ukraine's third attack on the crossing in a week. Ukrainian open-source channels posted the images, taken on November 19, showing damage to the road deck — one span has fallen into the sea — and to the railway line running alongside it. Ukraine has now struck the bridge three times in a week, on the nights of November 16, 17 and 19, with the latest attack coming just hours before Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping met in Shenzhen. Rail traffic across the bridge was temporarily closed after the strikes but was reopened on November 19, while the bridge remains closed to car traffic. Video from a train crossing the bridge after the second attack had already shown the wrecked road span, and the new satellite images confirm the scale of the damage. The bridge is Russia's only direct land link to occupied Crimea and a key supply route for its forces, and Ukraine has made it a repeated target since 2022.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Kursk: 13 injured, including a child, and 98 buildings damaged
articles.description: Ukrainian drones struck the Russian city of Kursk on Thursday morning, injuring 13 people, including a 12-year-old boy pulled from the rubble of a private house, and damaging 98 buildings and 67 cars. The city's arbitration court, central library, medical college and a private clinic were among the buildings hit, according to regional governor Alexander Khinshtein.
articles.body: Ukrainian drones struck the Russian city of Kursk on Thursday morning, November 19, injuring 13 people, including a child, and damaging 98 buildings and 67 cars. Regional governor Alexander Khinshtein said eight women, four men and one child were hurt; rescuers pulled a 12-year-old boy from under the rubble of a private house in the north-west of the city, and two visitors to a private clinic suffered shrapnel wounds. Falling drone debris and the blast wave damaged apartment blocks, private houses and administrative buildings in the city centre, including the arbitration court, the central city library, the House of Everyday Services and a medical college. Kursk region, which borders Ukraine, is regularly attacked by Ukrainian forces, and the strike came on the same day Ukraine hit the Crimean Bridge for the third time in a week. The number of injured rose through the day as rescue work continued, from 11 in the morning to 13 by the evening.

articles.title: Russian drone kills one in Kyiv and damages the Dutch Embassy — days after a Russian drone crashed near it
articles.description: A Russian drone attack on Kyiv killed one person and damaged the Dutch Embassy, just after the APEC summit ended. Meduza also reports Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge with missiles made by a Dutch company — and two days later, a Russian drone crashed near the Dutch Embassy in Kyiv.
articles.body: A Russian drone attack on Kyiv killed one person and damaged the Dutch Embassy, Meduza reports, in a strike that came just after the APEC summit in Shenzhen ended. The attack is part of a pattern of Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital that have repeatedly hit diplomatic premises, and the European Union said it will summon Russia's ambassador over strikes on Kyiv that damaged embassies. In a separate report, Meduza says Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge with missiles made by a Dutch company — and two days later, a Russian drone crashed near the Dutch Embassy in Kyiv, a coincidence that has drawn attention in the Netherlands. The bridge strike, the third in a week, used long-range missiles that Ukraine has been deploying against Russian logistics in occupied Crimea. The back-to-back incidents underline how the war keeps spilling onto diplomatic ground: embassies in Kyiv have been damaged more than once, and European governments have protested each time.

articles.title: Moscow court extends political scientist Alexander Kynev's detention — he came to court on crutches, leg broken during arrest
articles.description: A Moscow court has extended the detention of Russian political scientist Alexander Kynev, who appeared in court on crutches and in a cast after his leg was broken during his arrest. Kynev is one of Russia's best-known election analysts, and his detention has drawn condemnation from colleagues.
articles.body: A Moscow court has extended the detention of Russian political scientist Alexander Kynev, Meduza reports. Kynev appeared in court on crutches and in a cast, after his leg was broken during his arrest — a detail that has sharpened the outcry from colleagues and rights advocates. Kynev is one of Russia's best-known independent election analysts, a frequent commentator on the country's electoral system and regional politics, and his prosecution fits a pattern of cases against academics and analysts who have criticised the authorities since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The court did not disclose the specific charges in the reporting, but the extension of his detention keeps him in custody while the investigation continues. His case is the latest in a series of prosecutions of public intellectuals in Russia, where the space for independent political analysis has narrowed sharply.

articles.title: Finland's entry restrictions keep seven Russian skaters out of the Helsinki Grand Prix — Putin says it 'erodes trust'
articles.description: Finland's entry restrictions have kept seven Russian figure skaters out of the Helsinki Grand Prix, and Vladimir Putin said the decision 'erodes trust.' The episode is the latest example of Russian athletes being shut out of international competition over the war in Ukraine.
articles.body: Finland's entry restrictions have kept seven Russian figure skaters out of the Helsinki Grand Prix, Meduza reports, and Vladimir Putin said the decision 'erodes trust.' The skaters were unable to travel to Finland for the competition under the restrictions Helsinki maintains on Russian nationals, a policy imposed after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Putin's comment frames the episode as a political slight rather than a sporting matter, part of the Kremlin's broader complaint that Russian athletes are being unfairly excluded from international sport. Russian athletes have been largely barred from international competition since 2022, competing only as neutrals in some events and under strict conditions, and the Helsinki case shows the restrictions now reach even events held in countries that once hosted Russian skaters routinely. The Grand Prix series is one of figure skating's main international circuits, and the absence of seven Russians reshapes the field.

articles.title: Wikipedia editors in Russia could face prosecution if authorities declare its foundation 'undesirable'
articles.description: Wikipedia editors in Russia could face criminal prosecution if the authorities declare the Wikimedia Foundation an 'undesirable' organisation, Meduza reports. The designation would criminalise cooperation with the foundation that runs the free encyclopedia, putting volunteer editors at legal risk.
articles.body: Wikipedia editors in Russia could face prosecution if the authorities declare the Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the free encyclopedia, an 'undesirable' organisation, Meduza reports. The 'undesirable' designation, a tool the Kremlin has used against foreign NGOs, media outlets and foundations, criminalises cooperation with the listed organisation and can carry prison terms. For Wikipedia, the threat would fall on the volunteer editors in Russia who write and maintain articles — including articles about the war in Ukraine that contradict the official Russian narrative. Russia has already fined Wikipedia repeatedly and tried to force it to delete content, and a designation would escalate the pressure from fines to criminal liability. The move would also fit the broader campaign against independent information in Russia, which this week saw the Duma pass a law restricting library access to books by 'foreign agents.' Wikipedia remains one of the most-used sources of information in Russia, and its Russian-language edition is a key battleground over the historical record.

articles.title: Russian State Duma approves the 2027–2029 federal budget in its second reading
articles.description: Russia's State Duma has approved the 2027–2029 federal budget in its second reading, Meduza reports. The budget sets the Kremlin's spending plans for the next three years, with the war in Ukraine continuing to dominate expenditure.
articles.body: Russia's State Duma has approved the federal budget for 2027 and the planning period of 2028–2029 in its second reading, Meduza reports. The second reading is the stage at which deputies consider amendments to the spending plans, and the budget now moves toward final adoption. The budget sets the Kremlin's fiscal course for the next three years, with military spending and the costs of the war in Ukraine continuing to dominate expenditure, alongside social obligations and the rising cost of servicing state debt. Deputies considered hundreds of amendments to the draft, including dozens concerning healthcare funding. The budget debate comes as Russia's economy strains under sanctions, high interest rates and the cost of the war, and as the government looks for new revenue sources. The final reading is expected to follow quickly, as the Duma routinely passes the budget before the end of the year.

articles.title: Kushner: US persuaded Russia of the need for Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine
articles.description: Jared Kushner says the United States has persuaded Russia of the need for security guarantees for Ukraine modelled on NATO's Article 5, speaking in Berlin where he and Steve Witkoff are meeting the Coalition of the Willing. The claim, if it holds, would be a significant shift — Moscow has long rejected any Western security guarantees for Kyiv — though no text or Russian confirmation has been published.
articles.body: Jared Kushner says the United States has persuaded Russia of the need for security guarantees for Ukraine modelled on NATO's Article 5, Ukrainska Pravda reports from Berlin, where Kushner and Steve Witkoff are meeting the Coalition of the Willing. An Article 5-style guarantee would mean an attack on Ukraine is treated as an attack on its guarantors — the closest thing to NATO membership without membership itself — and it has been a central Ukrainian demand throughout the diplomacy around ending the war. The claim, if it holds, would mark a significant shift, since Moscow has long rejected any Western security guarantees for Kyiv, and no text of an agreement or Russian confirmation has been published. Kushner also said Trump sent a 'very strong message' to Putin and Xi at the Shenzhen summit, according to CNN. The Berlin meeting comes as European leaders try to pin down what security guarantees would actually look like, and as Zelenskyy said Europeans will be included in future negotiation formats with the Russians. The guarantees question is now the central diplomatic issue: Kyiv wants binding commitments before any ceasefire, while Moscow has insisted on terms closer to capitulation.

articles.title: Politico: Trump has questioned whether further spending on military support for Ukraine is worthwhile
articles.description: Donald Trump has questioned whether further spending on military support for Ukraine is worthwhile, Politico reports, according to Ukrainska Pravda's lead story on Thursday evening. The report lands as the US president returns from the Shenzhen summit, where Ukraine was discussed but absent from the joint declaration.
articles.body: Donald Trump has questioned whether further spending on military support for Ukraine is worthwhile, Politico reports, in Ukrainska Pravda's lead story on Thursday evening. The report lands as the US president returns from the first-ever trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, where Ukraine was discussed in the leaders' remarks but was absent from the four-point joint declaration. The question of continued military aid has hung over the diplomacy for months: Kyiv depends on Western weapons and air-defence supplies, while Trump has repeatedly pressed allies to carry more of the burden and has tied aid to his push for a settlement. Any US pullback would shift the balance of the war and force European partners to fill the gap, which is why the Politico report is the most-read story on Pravda's homepage on Thursday evening. It also sits uneasily alongside Kushner's claim from Berlin that Washington has persuaded Moscow to accept Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine — a commitment that would be hard to square with cutting military support.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Europeans will be included in negotiation formats with the Russians
articles.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Europeans will be included in negotiation formats with the Russians, addressing a long-standing European complaint about being sidelined in the diplomacy around the war. The statement comes as the Coalition of the Willing meets in Berlin with Kushner and Witkoff.
articles.body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Europeans will be included in negotiation formats with the Russians, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The statement addresses one of the most persistent European complaints about the diplomacy around the war: that the continent most affected by the conflict has been sidelined while Washington and Moscow talk. It comes as the Coalition of the Willing meets in Berlin, with Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff at the table, to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine. Zelenskyy has repeatedly insisted that no settlement can be imposed over Kyiv's head and that Europe must be part of any deal, a position European leaders share after the Shenzhen summit produced a joint declaration that did not mention Ukraine at all. The practical shape of the formats — who sits at the table, and when — remains unclear, but the commitment is a signal to European capitals that their role is recognised. It also follows Zelenskyy's statement on Wednesday that Ukraine's battlefield positions are strong, citing the defence of Dobropillia and Kostiantynivka.

articles.title: Trump: Putin was angered by Zelenskyy over the attack on the Kerch Bridge
articles.description: Donald Trump says Vladimir Putin was angered by Volodymyr Zelenskyy over Ukraine's attack on the Kerch Bridge, according to Ukrainska Pravda. The remark came after Ukraine struck the bridge for the third time in a week, hours before the three leaders met in Shenzhen.
articles.body: Donald Trump says Vladimir Putin was angered by Volodymyr Zelenskyy over Ukraine's attack on the Kerch Bridge, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The remark came after Ukraine struck the bridge for the third time in a week, on the night of November 19, just hours before Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping sat down in Shenzhen. The timing of the strike — the third in seven days, following attacks on the nights of November 16 and 17 — was widely read as a deliberate signal from Kyiv ahead of the summit, demonstrating that Ukraine can still hit Russia's most symbolic infrastructure even as the great powers discuss its fate. Satellite images published on Thursday show a collapsed road span lying in the water, and rail traffic was briefly halted before reopening. Trump relayed Putin's anger without endorsing it, and the bridge did not appear in the four-point joint declaration the three leaders issued. The episode captures the tension at the heart of the summit: Ukraine was the subject of the talks but not a party to them, and its military actions continued regardless.

articles.title: Putin says he invited EU representatives to Moscow to discuss Ukraine
articles.description: Vladimir Putin says he has invited representatives of the European Union to Moscow to discuss Ukraine, according to Ukrainska Pravda. The invitation, if taken up, would be a rare direct channel between Moscow and Brussels, which have had almost no high-level contact since the full-scale invasion.
articles.body: Vladimir Putin says he has invited representatives of the European Union to Moscow to discuss Ukraine, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The invitation, if taken up, would open a rare direct channel between Moscow and Brussels, which have had almost no high-level contact since the full-scale invasion in 2022. It comes on the same day Zelenskyy said Europeans will be included in negotiation formats with the Russians, and as the Coalition of the Willing meets in Berlin to discuss security guarantees. Whether the EU accepts is unclear: Brussels has insisted that talks must include Kyiv and that Russia must first show willingness to stop the fighting, and a Moscow visit would be politically sensitive for any European official. The invitation may be more about optics than substance — a signal from Putin, fresh from the Shenzhen summit, that he is open to talking to Europe on his own terms. It also follows the summit's joint declaration, which called for UN reform and dialogue on nuclear risks but said nothing about Ukraine.

articles.title: EU to summon Russia's ambassador over Kyiv strikes that damaged embassies
articles.description: The European Union will summon Russia's ambassador over strikes on Kyiv that damaged embassies, including the Dutch Embassy, Ukrainska Pravda reports. A Russian drone attack on the capital killed one person and damaged the Dutch mission, days after another Russian drone crashed near it.
articles.body: The European Union will summon Russia's ambassador over strikes on Kyiv that damaged embassies, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The summons follows a Russian drone attack on the Ukrainian capital that killed one person and damaged the Dutch Embassy, and comes days after another Russian drone crashed near the same embassy. Summoning an ambassador is a formal diplomatic protest, and the EU's move signals that attacks on diplomatic premises — which are protected under international law — are being treated as a distinct escalation. Embassies in Kyiv have been damaged more than once during the war, and European governments have protested each time, but a coordinated EU summons raises the diplomatic stakes. The move also comes as the EU weighs its role in the diplomacy around the war, with Zelenskyy saying Europeans will be included in future negotiation formats and Putin saying he has invited EU representatives to Moscow. The embassy strikes underline that the war's violence continues even as the great powers talk about peace in Shenzhen.

articles.title: GTA VI is out worldwide — and players placed a record 20 million pre-orders
articles.description: Grand Theft Auto VI launched worldwide on Thursday for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, and Sensor Tower estimates players placed about 20 million pre-orders before release, with numbers rising by roughly a million copies a day in the final stretch. The game holds a 99 on Metacritic, tying the highest score in the site's history, and had already banked more than $1.65 billion before anyone played it.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI launched worldwide on Thursday, November 19, for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, and players placed a record number of pre-orders ahead of release. Analytics firm Sensor Tower estimates about 20 million pre-orders were placed before the launch, with the figure rising by roughly one million copies a day in the final days. The game, set in the fictional state of Leonida inspired by Florida, holds a 99 on Metacritic — tying The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game in the site's history — and Sensor Tower estimates it had already generated more than $1.65 billion before launch. Rockstar's release is the biggest entertainment launch in years: rival publishers cleared their calendars around it, with Fable and Squadron 42 pushed into 2027, and the game is expected to break first-week sales records across the industry. A PC version has still not been announced, and Take-Two chief Strauss Zelnick has warned that AI-generated unofficial PC ports are a new piracy threat the publisher is watching closely.

articles.title: Rockstar developers fear layoffs after GTA VI launches, programmer says
articles.description: Rockstar Games employees are afraid of losing their jobs after Grand Theft Auto VI launches, according to programmer Nestor Uriarte. The atmosphere at the studio is calm for now and nothing points to cuts being prepared, but the wider crisis in the games industry is feeding the anxiety.
articles.body: Rockstar Games employees are afraid of losing their jobs once Grand Theft Auto VI is out, according to programmer Nestor Uriarte, GameMAG reports. Uriarte said staff at the studio fear layoffs after the game's release, even though the atmosphere is calm for now and nothing indicates cuts are being prepared. The worry reflects the wider crisis in the games industry, where studios have shed tens of thousands of jobs in the past two years — often right after a big launch, when teams are restructured and contractors let go. Rockstar has spent years and a reported fortune building GTA VI, and the game's record-breaking pre-orders and 99 Metacritic score suggest it will be a commercial triumph, but that has not eased the fear among the people who made it. The report lands on launch day, as the game goes on sale worldwide and the industry watches to see whether Rockstar's success will be followed by the same post-launch cuts seen at other major studios.

articles.title: GTA VI is locked at 30fps on consoles — and Digital Foundry found it drops to 18fps on Xbox Series S
articles.description: Grand Theft Auto VI runs at a single graphics mode targeting 30 frames per second on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, including PS5 Pro, Rockstar has confirmed — there is no 60fps performance mode. Digital Foundry's tests found the game mostly holds 30fps on Series X but drops as low as 18fps on the less powerful Series S.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI runs at a single graphics mode targeting 30 frames per second on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, Rockstar Games has confirmed — including on PlayStation 5 Pro, where owners should not expect a 60fps performance mode. Rockstar explained the 30fps cap to TechRadar, and Digital Foundry's technical tests back up the decision: on Xbox Series X the game holds its 30fps target most of the time, but on the less powerful Xbox Series S it drops as low as 18 frames per second in demanding scenes. Digital Foundry's John Linneman, who played the game on PS5 and PS5 Pro, still called it the most visually impressive game of the generation among realistic-looking releases, and praised its open world. The 30fps limit has been one of the few criticisms of a launch otherwise dominated by record review scores and pre-orders, and it has fuelled debate about whether the game will eventually get a 60fps mode or a PC version, where higher frame rates would be possible. For now, Rockstar has given no indication that either is coming.

articles.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's lead writer left Sandfall Interactive back in July
articles.description: Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, the lead writer of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 — one of 2026's most acclaimed games — left developer Sandfall Interactive back in July, she has revealed in an interview with GamesBeat. The departure only became public now, tied to her selection for the BAFTA Breakthrough US programme.
articles.body: Jennifer Svedberg-Yen, the lead writer of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, left developer Sandfall Interactive back in July, GameMAG reports — but the departure only became public now. Svedberg-Yen revealed it in an interview with GamesBeat tied to her selection for the BAFTA Breakthrough US programme, which supports emerging talent in film, TV and games. Expedition 33 was one of 2026's most acclaimed releases, praised above all for its writing and story, and Svedberg-Yen was central to that success as the game's lead writer. Her exit raises questions about the future of the series, since the game's narrative voice was so closely identified with her work, though neither she nor the studio has said what she will do next. The news lands in a week dominated by GTA VI, but for the industry it is a significant departure: Expedition 33 was a breakout hit for a small French studio, and losing its lead writer is a reminder of how fragile small-team success can be.

articles.title: Sony wins UK PlayStation Store pricing case as court throws out the £2 billion claim
articles.description: Sony has won its case in the UK over PlayStation Store prices, after the Competition Appeal Tribunal fully rejected a class action seeking almost £2 billion — about $2.6 billion — from the company. The claim argued Sony abused its dominance by charging excessive prices on its digital store.
articles.body: Sony has won its case in the United Kingdom over PlayStation Store prices, GameMAG reports. The Competition Appeal Tribunal fully rejected the class action, in which Sony Interactive Entertainment was accused of abusing its dominant position and customers sought almost £2 billion — about $2.6 billion — in damages. The claimants argued that Sony charged excessive prices on the PlayStation Store by taking a 30% commission and restricting competition from other digital retailers. The tribunal's decision clears Sony of the claim entirely, and it is a significant victory for the platform holder at a time when digital storefront fees are under scrutiny around the world — from the Epic Games cases against Apple and Google to regulatory probes in Europe. For PlayStation owners, the ruling means no compensation is coming and the store's pricing model stands. The decision is likely to be cited by other platform holders facing similar claims, and it underlines how hard it is to win excessive-pricing cases against digital stores in UK courts.

articles.title: The Blood of Dawnwalker gets update 1.2 with new content after player criticism
articles.description: Rebel Wolves has released update 1.2 for its vampire role-playing game The Blood of Dawnwalker, adding new content and answering player criticism, alongside a new trailer. The update is the studio's second major round of post-launch support for the game.
articles.body: Rebel Wolves has released update 1.2 for its role-playing game The Blood of Dawnwalker, GameMAG reports, alongside a new trailer. The update adds new content and addresses criticism from players since the game launched, as the Polish studio — founded by veterans of CD Projekt Red — continues its post-launch support. The Blood of Dawnwalker is a dark fantasy RPG built around a vampire protagonist, and its launch drew attention as one of the most ambitious debut projects from a new studio in years. Update 1.2 is the latest step in the studio's effort to refine the game in response to feedback, a process that has become standard for big RPG launches. The trailer accompanying the update shows the new material in action, and the studio has signalled further updates are planned.

articles.title: Exodus shows off June Aslan — the female version of its hero — ahead of April 2027 launch
articles.description: Hasbro and Archetype Entertainment have shown new gameplay from Exodus, introducing June Aslan, the female version of the game's hero, ahead of its release on April 7, 2027 for PC and consoles. The sci-fi RPG from BioWare veterans is pitched as a spiritual successor to Mass Effect.
articles.body: Hasbro and Archetype Entertainment have shown new gameplay from Exodus, introducing June Aslan — the female version of the game's hero — ahead of its release on April 7, 2027 for PC and consoles, GameMAG reports. Exodus is a science-fiction role-playing game from a team built around BioWare veterans, and it is pitched as a spiritual successor to Mass Effect, with a story about humanity's search for a new home among the stars. The new footage shows June Aslan, one of two versions of the protagonist players can choose, and gives the fullest look yet at the game's combat and world. The April 2027 date puts Exodus in a crowded window for big RPGs, but the Mass Effect pedigree of its team — led by James Ohlen, a veteran of the original trilogy — has made it one of the most anticipated games of next year. The reveal is the latest in a run of pre-launch showings as the studio builds toward release.

articles.title: Anthropic debuts at nearly $2 trillion as shares jump 34% — the biggest IPO ever
articles.description: Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, made its stock market debut on Thursday valued at nearly $2 trillion, with shares opening at $111.50 — 34% above the IPO price — before slipping slightly. The listing is the largest public debut of all time, and almost all of the company's employees are now millionaires on paper.
articles.body: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, made its stock market debut on Thursday valued at nearly $2 trillion, in what CNN calls the largest public listing of all time. Shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, then slipped slightly in early trading, and almost all Anthropic employees are now millionaires on paper. Founded just five years ago, Anthropic has become one of the central players in the AI race, competing with OpenAI and Google while building a reputation for safety-focused development. The debut caps a week in which AI dominated business news, from chip export controls to the Suno music lawsuits, and it comes a day after CNN reported the listing could be worth as much as $1.4 trillion — the market priced it higher still. A valuation near $2 trillion places the young company among the most valuable in the world on day one and tests whether public markets will sustain AI valuations previously reserved for the largest incumbents. The listing is being followed live by CNN as one of the day's top stories.

articles.title: Iowans brace for a lead dust cloud as the Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals
articles.description: The US Army plans to detonate about 5 tons of unstable bomb-making chemicals at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Friday, and some Iowa residents fear a cloud of lead dust could contaminate the area. Officials recommend some residents of nearby Middletown vacate, schools and the library in Mediapolis will close, and the EPA approved an emergency permit for the blast on November 13.
articles.body: The US Army plans to detonate about 5 tons of unstable bomb-making chemicals at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Friday, November 20, and some Iowa residents are worried a cloud of lead dust could cause environmental contamination and health problems. The material is lead azide, discovered in several dozen barrels in March after the plant paused operations for a review; the Army says it has become unstable and might explode if moved. Officials recommend that some residents of nearby Middletown, home to nearly 400 people, vacate the area, and schools and the public library in Mediapolis, less than 20 miles away, will close on Friday. The detonation is expected to produce an air plume with lead-containing particles that will disperse and settle on the ground, lingering for no more than an hour depending on wind speed; the Army says modelling predicts lead levels in the air will stay well below the level at which the EPA would require protective action. The Iowa Department of Agriculture advised bringing animals, hay bales and water indoors, and maps showing the potential drift are being updated with weather forecasts. Iowa US Senator-elect Josh Turek is among those calling for the detonation to be delayed, arguing the public needs to understand the health impacts better. The EPA approved an emergency permit for the blast on November 13.

articles.title: Trump admin tried to get free legal work from a major law firm for the arch and Kennedy Center battles
articles.description: The Trump administration unsuccessfully tried to get the major law firm Kirkland & Ellis to do pro bono work supporting the president's triumphal arch project and the renaming of the Kennedy Center, according to a letter the firm sent to three Democratic lawmakers on November 5. The firm says it turned both requests down, though it did nearly $12 million of free legal work after cutting a deal to provide $125 million in free services to Trump-backed causes.
articles.body: The Trump administration unsuccessfully tried to get the major law firm Kirkland & Ellis to do pro bono work supporting projects President Donald Trump has championed — his triumphal arch and the renaming of the Kennedy Center — according to a letter the firm sent to three Democratic lawmakers on November 5 and obtained by CNN. The seven-page letter to Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal, California Senator Adam Schiff and Maryland Representative Jamie Raskin says the firm helped the Trump administration and several federal agencies with pro bono work after cutting a deal to avoid a White House-prompted freeze-out, and did nearly $12 million of free legal work following the agreement to provide $125 million in free legal services to causes Trump supported. But the firm says it turned down the requests to work on the Kennedy Center renaming and to represent a veterans' group that supported the arch. The episode is part of a wider White House effort last year to enlist several law firms in pro bono work, after the president issued executive orders targeting firms — later blocked by courts as unconstitutional — that reshaped the legal industry in Washington. Democrats are still seeking details of the other law-firm deals, and the pro bono work is likely to be a focus of congressional investigations in the new Congress.

articles.title: UN's top court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide — the first time it has ever held a state accountable
articles.description: The International Court of Justice has found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against the Rohingya minority, by nine votes to six — the first time in the court's 80-year history it has held a state accountable for genocide. The court ordered Myanmar to pay reparations and to allow the safe, voluntary and dignified return of the Rohingya to their homes.
articles.body: The International Court of Justice has found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against the Rohingya minority, in a historic judgment that marks the first time the court has held a state accountable for genocide in its 80-year history. The decision, by nine votes to six, was handed down on Thursday in a case brought by Gambia, and survivors of the atrocities have waited almost a decade to hear it. The court ordered Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingya, including to allow and facilitate their safe, voluntary and dignified return to their places of residence and the reunification of families, and to return all property lost or damaged. The ruling comes at a time when the broader idea of international justice is under fire from the Trump administration, and it will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar — including for the Shenzhen summit's declaration, which said the International Criminal Court must not abuse its jurisdiction. The ICJ's rulings are final and binding, but the court has no power to enforce them, and CNN has reached out to Myanmar's military-backed government for comment. The US State Department said it is studying the decision, and UN human rights chief Volker Türk called the judgment 'historic.'

articles.title: 'Eighty-one minutes with strongman friends': takeaways from Trump's sit-down with Putin and Xi
articles.description: CNN's takeaways from the first-ever Trump-Putin-Xi summit in Shenzhen: the meeting lasted 81 minutes, and diplomatic breakthroughs were not the point — the talks themselves were the deliverable. The three leaders issued a four-point declaration, but it settled none of the wars or arms questions on the agenda.
articles.body: CNN's takeaways from the first-ever trilateral summit between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen: the meeting lasted 81 minutes, and diplomatic breakthroughs were not the point — the talks themselves were the deliverable. The three leaders issued a four-point joint declaration covering UN reform, refined petroleum supplies, limits on the International Criminal Court's jurisdiction and dialogue on nuclear risks, but it contained no agreement on Ukraine, Iran or nuclear arms, and no trade deal. The summit's symbolism was the story: three great powers meeting in a format that deliberately excluded smaller nations, with Kyiv and its European partners watching for any deal struck over Ukraine's head. Trump also met Putin separately for about 40 minutes and agreed with Xi to extend their trade truce, though neither side disclosed the terms. The leaders held no joint press conference, and Trump left Shenzhen for Washington soon after, planning to brief the press on Friday. CNN's analysis notes the summit established a new three-leader format, but its published commitments are narrower than the ambitions expressed before the doors closed.

articles.title: Fiona, the globally adored hippo, dies at Cincinnati Zoo
articles.description: Fiona, the hippopotamus who became a global celebrity after her premature birth at the Cincinnati Zoo, has died, CNN reports in breaking news. Fiona won millions of fans around the world and became one of the most famous animals in captivity.
articles.body: Fiona, the hippopotamus who became a global celebrity after her premature birth at the Cincinnati Zoo, has died, CNN reports in breaking news on Thursday. Fiona was born six weeks early in 2017, weighing just 29 pounds, and her fight for survival — documented by the zoo in videos and updates — won her millions of fans around the world. She grew into one of the most famous animals in captivity, with merchandise, books and a social media following, and she became a symbol of the zoo's conservation work. Her death was reported as breaking news on CNN's homepage on Thursday afternoon, alongside the day's political and business stories. The zoo has not yet disclosed the cause of death in the initial reporting.

articles.title: CNN exclusive: FAA policy change let a contractor work with little oversight before the nationwide ground stop
articles.description: A CNN exclusive reports on the FAA policy change behind a contractor working with little oversight before the nationwide ground stop on November 13. The report is the latest development in the cascade of tech outages that has dominated the news this month.
articles.body: A CNN exclusive reports on the Federal Aviation Administration policy change behind a contractor working with little oversight before the nationwide ground stop on November 13, which grounded flights across the United States and caused travel delays that persisted through the weekend. The exclusive is the latest development in the cascade of technology outages that has dominated the news this month — from the global Microsoft outage to the FAA ground stop and glitches at Workday, Chase Bank, United Airlines and Apple's systems. The FAA has since paused installations of Juniper routers, the equipment at the centre of the ground stop, while the investigation continues. CNN's reporting on the contractor's oversight adds a new dimension to the story: it was not only a technical failure but a question of how the agency supervises the private companies that maintain its systems. The ground stop has become a case study in the fragility of critical infrastructure, and it is now a subject of congressional interest as well.

articles.title: Warner Music tops $2 billion in a quarter for the first time as streaming jumps 14.7%
articles.description: Warner Music Group generated $2.001 billion in revenue in calendar Q3 2026 — the first time its quarterly revenues have crossed $2 billion, beating the previous record of $1.868 billion set a year earlier. Recorded music subscription streaming rose 14.7% year on year to $804 million, with Madonna, Charli XCX, Bruno Mars and Linkin Park among the quarter's top sellers.
articles.body: Warner Music Group has generated total revenues of $2.001 billion in the three months ended September 30, 2026 — calendar Q3, the company's fiscal Q4 — the first time its quarterly revenues have crossed the $2 billion mark. The figure beats WMG's previous record of $1.868 billion, set in calendar Q3 2025, and was up 7.5% year on year at constant currency. Recorded music revenues rose 7.3% to $1.639 billion, and within that, subscription streaming revenues were up 14.7% year on year to $804 million, showing the streaming engine still growing at a double-digit pace. Top sellers in the quarter included Madonna, Number_i, Charli XCX, Bruno Mars and Linkin Park. WMG also said full-year fiscal 2026 revenues hit an all-time high of $7.437 billion, up 10.9%, with net income nearly doubling to $735 million. The results land in a big week for the company: chief executive Robert Kyncl is due to deliver the keynote at CES 2027 in January, billed as the first by a music-industry leader.

articles.title: Live Nation's Rapino talks AI strategy and subscription ambitions for its 14m-member All Access programme
articles.description: Live Nation chief executive Michael Rapino used the company's 2026 investor presentation to set out its AI strategy and its subscription ambitions for All Access, its 14-million-member programme. The presentation came five days after Live Nation reported third-quarter revenues of $10.1 billion, up 19% year on year.
articles.body: Live Nation chief executive Michael Rapino used the company's 2026 investor presentation to set out its AI strategy and its subscription ambitions for All Access, its 14-million-member programme, Music Business Worldwide reports. The presentation came five days after Live Nation reported third-quarter revenues of $10.1 billion, up 19% year on year, underlining the live giant's scale as it looks for its next growth engine. Rapino's focus on AI covers how the company uses the technology across ticketing, marketing and the fan experience, while the All Access programme — a subscription-style membership for concertgoers — is being positioned as a recurring-revenue business alongside the core concerts and ticketing operations. The investor day is one of the most closely watched events in the live music calendar, since Live Nation's scale makes its strategy a proxy for the health of the whole concert business. The company's pitch is that live music keeps growing even as recorded music matures, and that subscriptions and AI can deepen the relationship with fans who already buy millions of tickets a year.
