Eight holiday songs already hold spots in the Billboard Hot 100's top 50, and the newest arrival is Olivia Rodrigo's first-ever holiday song, 'Take Me Home (4 Christmas)', which debuts at No. 32. Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' leads the seasonal pack, jumping from No. 37 to No. 14, while Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' climbs from No. 39 to No. 18 — Wham! pulling a little farther ahead of Carey this week. Bobby Helms' 'Jingle Bell Rock' re-enters at No. 28, reaching its 69th total week on the chart nearly 70 years after its release, and Brenda Lee's 'Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree' follows at No. 30. The Hot 100 carries a November 21 date and tracks listening and sales from November 6 to 12, so this is an early snapshot of the season, not a verdict — but the holiday takeover is already under way.

articles.title: CL signs with Teddy's THEBLACKLABEL, first release due this month
articles.description: Singer CL has signed with THEBLACKLABEL, the label founded by producer Teddy in 2015, Billboard reported on November 13. Her first release under the deal arrives this month. Financial terms have not been made public.
articles.body: Singer CL has signed with THEBLACKLABEL, the label founded by producer Teddy in 2015, Billboard reported on November 13. Her first release under the deal arrives this month, though the report did not give its title, format or release day. Financial terms have not been made public. The move puts the former 2NE1 leader with one of K-pop's most influential producers: Teddy built his reputation crafting hits for BLACKPINK, BIGBANG and 2NE1 itself, and THEBLACKLABEL has become a home for artists looking for a more producer-led setup. For CL, whose solo career has moved between labels and independent releases, the signing is a fresh start with a heavyweight behind her.

articles.title: "AI DJs Completely Kill My Groove"
articles.author: Lauren Goode
articles.description: A first-person field test of the AI DJ features Spotify and YouTube Music are pushing into everyone's playlists — directly relevant to how music fans actually experience streaming now, and a cautionary tale about AI features that interrupt rather than enhance listening.
articles.body:
WIRED software reporter Lauren Goode, a self-described beta-feature enthusiast who uses YouTube Music as her main streaming service, tried living with the synthetic DJ hosts both YouTube Music and Spotify now build into their apps — and ended up turning both of them off. YouTube's version, called "Beyond the Beat" and available through YouTube Labs, randomly interrupts a queue for about 30 seconds between songs to explain the track, set up a vibe shift, and offer context. Spotify introduced its own AI DJ back in 2023 and expanded it in November 2026 with more host personalities and extra controls over the commentary.

The breaking point came during a pop-divas workout playlist. After a Slayyyter track, YouTube's AI DJ launched into a long, platitude-filled monologue about the next Charli XCX song — mispronouncing the artist's name as "Charli XXC" and offering generic commentary with no real substance. Goode's verdict is that the effect is closer to interruption than curation: stilted banter, confidently wrong song trivia, and filler words like "um" and "like" meant to sound human, all breaking the flow of the music the features are supposed to celebrate. Spotify's version fared no better in her testing, despite its head start and its November expansion to eight English-language voices.

The piece's larger point is about where generative AI is being bolted on. Both features remain optional betas that listeners can disable, and Goode argues that is exactly what most listeners will do: the synthetic hosts strip away the human nuance, serendipity, and cultural context that made radio DJs and human curators valuable in the first place, reducing songs to data points wrapped in awkward small talk. For anyone building or marketing music, it is a useful reality check on the gap between the demo promise of "AI curation" and what listeners actually tolerate.

articles.title: "They left the Kennedy Center to survive. It was an artistic rebirth."
articles.author: Philip Kennicott
articles.description: A vivid account of how the Washington National Opera rebuilt itself from zero after walking away from the Kennedy Center — and why the enforced exile produced better, bolder art. A strong arts-institution story with direct lessons for any independent arts organisation.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's takeover of the Kennedy Center nearly destroyed the Washington National Opera. After Trump stacked the centre's board with loyalists, had himself appointed chairman in 2025, and then put his own name on the venue — a living memorial to John F. Kennedy — ticket sales fell, and the opera's board concluded there was no viable way to continue an association dating back to the centre's opening in 1971. In January 2026 the board voted to leave, and the company scrambled to finish the last two operas of the 2025–26 season at George Washington University's Lisner Auditorium in March.

The break was total. The opera had been affiliated with the Kennedy Center since 2011, and under that arrangement the centre provided all of its infrastructure — so when it declared independence in January it had no employees, no insurance, no bank accounts, and no infrastructure at all. It also lost the centre's $2.75 million annual subsidy. General director Timothy O'Leary describes it as a do-or-die situation: the company had to rebuild the entire institution while keeping the show going, and just eight weeks after declaring independence it staged a sold-out performance of Scott Joplin's Treemonisha, which the New York Times called a miracle. More than 3,000 donors from 47 states have since chipped in, including one anonymous $500,000 gift.

Now, Kennicott argues, the hardship has ignited a genuine artistic rebirth. The company has turned DAR Constitution Hall — Washington's largest concert hall, an acoustically problematic space never designed for theatre — into a dynamic contemporary opera house, decking over the main seating area and building a three-quarter thrust "Revolutionary Stage" ringed with café-style seating. Its fall residency there pairs a traditional but explosively powerful new Madama Butterfly (Nov 7–20) with a new staging of John Adams's Nixon in China (Nov 14–21), which Kennicott calls not only one of the greatest operas of the past century but an oracular vision of a world we are only beginning to inhabit. The 2026–27 season, its first as a fully independent company in its 70th anniversary year, runs five full-length productions across five venues — Constitution Hall, Arena Stage, Shakespeare Theatre Company's Harman Hall, Strathmore, and its own Takoma Park studio theatre — with 27 performances, down from 38 in 2024–25, but with more different works and star singers including Renée Fleming, Thomas Hampson, and Isabel Leonard. Kennicott's conclusion: the company is making art that outclasses and transcends the politics that displaced it.

articles.title: "The Radical Intimacies of Ryûsuke Hamaguchi"
articles.author: Justin Chang
articles.description: A rich, intimate profile of the Drive My Car director and his ambitious new three-hour film about caregiving, mortality, and radical empathy — part biography, part masterclass in how he makes actors and audiences truly pay attention to each other.
articles.body:
Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, 47, the Japanese director whose Drive My Car (2021) won the Oscar for Best International Feature and made him only the third Japanese filmmaker ever nominated for Best Director, has made a new film, All of a Sudden, that tackles caregiving, illness, and mortality head-on. The profile follows Chang's conversations with Hamaguchi in Tokyo and Cannes as the film — Japan's official Oscars submission for Best International Feature — heads for its US release. Its unusual source is a book of letters between philosopher Makiko Miyano, who had metastatic breast cancer, and medical anthropologist Maho Isono; the two women met in 2018, corresponded as Miyano's health declined, and the book was published in September 2019, a couple of months after Miyano's death.

Hamaguchi told Chang he was moved viscerally by the book but doubted it could be filmed, since so much of the correspondence was abstract — until the French company Cinéfrance Studios proposed a co-production. Working with French screenwriter Léa Le Dimna, he set the story at a nursing home in suburban Paris run by Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira), and built the film around Humanitude, a real care methodology for vulnerable patients, especially those with dementia, that stresses relationship-centred, hands-on treatment: direct eye contact, calm encouraging speech, gentle touch, and standing upright. Marie-Lou wants her overworked staff to adopt it; they resist its time-consuming, touchy-feely demands. Her life changes when she meets Mari Morisaki (Tao Okamoto), a Japanese experimental theatre director with terminal cancer, and the two women's friendship — intellectual, emotional, and possibly romantic — becomes the film's centre, including a long overnight conversation along the Seine that Hamaguchi modelled on Éric Rohmer's My Night at Maud's.

The piece also traces Hamaguchi's formation: a chubby manga-and-movies kid who saw The NeverEnding Story as his first film in a theatre, tore through Spielberg and Cameron on VHS, then discovered Cassavetes (whose Husbands thrilled him with its rawness) and Rohmer at university; a failed attempt to enter Tokyo University's film programme, a thesis on Cassavetes, and film school at Tokyo University of the Arts, where a Kiyoshi Kurosawa class taught him that the camera is an acutely observant recording machine — "there is almost a documentary power to the camera in itself" — and his films have tried to "create the conditions" that fool it into documenting fiction. His rehearsal method, born from an actor's suggestion to read lines flatly and repeatedly until theatricality falls away, descends from Bresson. And the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, which struck while he was finishing his four-hour student film Intimacies, sent him to the devastated region to film survivors for a documentary trilogy — an experience that taught him documentaries have a fiction element too, and that being in front of the camera himself was the only fair way to film other people's hurt. The film's Cannes premiere in May ended with Efira and Okamoto sharing the Best Actress prize, and a Variety critic said it "achieves a kind of levitating grace." Hamaguchi's own coda is about burnout: the Drive My Car awards tour left him feeling he was "becoming a rather unpleasant person," shutting people out — and All of a Sudden, a story about caregivers whose will and resources are sapped by the system, is his way of reclaiming unhurried time and attention, for himself and for his characters.

articles.title: "A Star on Planet Earth" (Timothée Chalamet, Vanity Fair Holiday 2026 cover story)
articles.author: Mark Guiducci
articles.description: The Holiday 2026 cover story on the defining young movie star of the moment, built around a striking Iceland shoot and a candid conversation about Dune: Part Three, creative ambition, and the Knicks — a good culture read on fame, craft, and choosing the work over the persona.
articles.body:
Timothée Chalamet is Vanity Fair's Holiday 2026 cover star, photographed by Aidan Zamiri over three days in Iceland and interviewed by the magazine's global editorial director Mark Guiducci, following an October conversation between the two. Rather than a conventional celebrity portrait session, Chalamet helped shape the shoot as something closer to a film or music video, citing Terrence Malick's The Tree of Life as the biggest visual inspiration and saying the process of creating the images mattered almost as much as the photographs themselves.

The biggest professional subject is Dune: Part Three, which arrives in North American theatres and IMAX on December 18, 2026 (December 16 internationally) and concludes Denis Villeneuve's trilogy. The film picks up nearly two decades after Paul Atreides takes control of the Imperium; Paul is now an emperor confronting the consequences of his rule as political threats, betrayal, and personal conflict close in. Chalamet describes making it as more isolated and psychologically demanding than the earlier films: he studied historical leaders whose ambition curdled into destructiveness, researched megalomaniacs to understand Paul's rise, and even shaved his familiar curls for the role's increasingly austere turn. The through-line is Frank Herbert's Dune Messiah warning about charismatic leadership and cults of personality.

The conversation ranges well beyond the franchise. Chalamet talks about his devotion to the New York Knicks — he describes himself as living two lives, one as an actor and one as a Knicks fan, and says the team embodies New York's identity in a way that goes beyond sport — and about the films that shaped him: The Tree of Life, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, Cloud Atlas, and the experimental documentary Koyaanisqatsi, choices that reveal a taste for work that experiments with structure, emotion, and scale. Directors who have worked with him weigh in too: Villeneuve speaks about his growing ambition, Greta Gerwig about an actor who needs creative freedom and room to keep a scene alive. Guiducci's portrait is of a star whose fame keeps growing while he stays guarded about his private life, letting the performances do the talking — from Call Me by Your Name and Lady Bird through Wonka, A Complete Unknown, and Marty Supreme (for which he was the Best Actor frontrunner at the March 2026 Oscars, losing to Michael B. Jordan for Sinners) — and who hints at a future collaboration with a prominent filmmaker he won't yet name.

articles.title: "Gracie Abrams: 'I Was Thrown Into the Deepest End Possible'" (The Rolling Stone Interview)
articles.author: Alex Morris
articles.description: A live, intimate Rolling Stone Interview with one of pop's defining young songwriters, recorded at New York's Cherry Lane Theatre — on her acting debut, getting offline, and the album that just gave her her first No. 1.
articles.body:
Last month Gracie Abrams joined Rolling Stone's residency at New York's historic Cherry Lane Theatre for a live edition of its deep-dive conversation series, The Rolling Stone Interview, speaking with Alex Morris. The conversation, published November 17, ranges across her acting debut, her relationship with being online, and why she can't wait to get back on the road. Her latest album, Daughter From Hell, is her most ambitious and musically varied offering to date — and a reflection of the perspective that comes from entering adulthood.

The album arrived in July 2026 and debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, Abrams's first-ever chart-topping album, with 15 tracks produced with Aaron Dessner of The National, her longtime collaborator. Abrams describes the record as an exploration of what she calls the "in-between quality" of your twenties — "one foot in a past life and one foot in the future" — written after a quiet period following the end of her tour, when being in your twenties "can feel lonely in a new way and it can feel thrilling in a new way." Collaborators on the album include Justin Vernon (Bon Iver), her best friend and songwriting partner Audrey Hobert, and her partner Paul Mescal, who co-wrote the track "Imaginary Friend."

The interview's most quoted moment concerns the three months Abrams spent filming her first feature, Please, the latest film from Babygirl director Halina Reijn — she released the album the day before flying to Berlin to shoot it. "I was thrown into the deepest end possible," she says of the experience, "and then it felt weirdly more relaxing than a lot of other parts of my life have felt over the past few years. I think it was a relief to spend three months not thinking about myself and about presentation." Morris draws out Abrams's signature humour and her candour about the challenge of marketing herself, the pressure of constant self-presentation, and how she is trying to give herself some grace — the portrait of a 27-year-old who came up posting bedroom recordings online, opened Taylor Swift's Eras Tour, and is now deliberately stepping out of the pop-star frame to try something harder.

articles.title: "How a Bunch of YouTube Auteurs Are Reinventing Hollywood"
articles.description: The summer's two biggest box-office surprises were micro-budget horror films by twenty-something YouTubers — and Hollywood is now scouting YouTube for its next directors. A sharp, fun piece on how the creator economy is becoming the film industry's talent pipeline.
articles.body:
The mad scramble for Imax tickets to The Odyssey and the Marvel Cinematic Universe's resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand New Day were supposed to be the stories of the 2026 summer movie season. Instead, the biggest buzz belonged to two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs. First came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which earned well over $150 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows Bear, a meek young man who yearns for a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true; by turns moody, funny, and shocking, it proved audiences are hungry for something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch-comedy channel That's a Bad Idea.

Then came Backrooms, from 21-year-old Kane Parsons, which earned over $120 million worldwide on a $10 million budget, surpassing Marty Supreme as A24's highest-grossing movie ever. Parsons gained a cult following as a teenager experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics; a series of shorts he made in his teens culminated in the feature, which picks up the story of his earlier YouTube videos — themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore about haunted liminal spaces. It stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé running a failing furniture warehouse who stumbles through a wall into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways. Critics have read it as a commentary on generative AI, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that don't make sense; Parsons has spoken out against AI several times since release, calling it "a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot."

The article's argument is that this is a structural shift, not a fluke. Parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that YouTube is "the only viable avenue" for long-form filmmakers seeking mainstream respect — "I don't think there's a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film" — and that among twentysomething directors entering the industry today, "it's very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now… who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube." Studios have noticed: after a screening of Barker's Obsession at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival, A24 and Neon entered a bidding war before Focus Features picked it up for roughly $15 million, and Netflix reportedly lost a bid to take it straight to streaming. The piece also name-checks Zach Cregger — sketch-comedy beginnings with The Whitest Kids U' Know, following 2025's Weapons with a 2026 Resident Evil adaptation — as part of the same wave. The conclusion: while Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a new wave of artists are betting on themselves, and some are winning. (Note: Wired's piece cites higher grosses — $500M+ and $400M — but other trackers, including Box Office Mojo, put the totals nearer $156M and $126M, so the lower figures are used here.)

articles.title: Russia's State Duma passes law restricting library access to books by 'foreign agents' — 380-0, in three minutes
articles.description: Russia's State Duma has passed a law restricting access to books by 'foreign agents' in the country's libraries, approving it in its second and third readings on Wednesday. The entire debate took three minutes, according to the news outlet RBC, and the bill passed 380-0 with no votes against.
articles.body: Russia's State Duma has passed a law restricting access to books by 'foreign agents' in the country's libraries, approving it in its second and third readings on Wednesday, November 18. The entire debate took three minutes, according to a correspondent for the news outlet RBC, and the bill passed 380-0, with no deputy voting against it. The law amends the rules governing libraries set out in the law 'On Librarianship' and imposes an '18+' age restriction on books by authors designated as 'foreign agents.' The bill was introduced in March 2024 and passed its first reading that June, before stalling for more than two years. Its passage is the latest step in the Kremlin's campaign against independent voices, extending the 'foreign agent' stigma from media and public life into the shelves of public libraries. For readers in Russia, works by some of the country's best-known writers, journalists and historians will now be formally restricted, and librarians will have to police access. The law is part of a broader package of repressive legislation adopted during the war, and it passed with the same unanimity that has characterised the Duma's wartime voting record.

articles.title: Prosecutors call for an end to the Khachaturyan sisters' murder case, saying they acted in self-defense
articles.description: Russian prosecutors have called for the murder case against the Khachaturyan sisters — Krestina, Angelina and Maria, accused of killing their abusive father in 2018 — to be dropped, saying they acted in self-defense. The case is one of the most high-profile domestic violence cases in modern Russian history, and the investigation into the sisters resumed in 2026.
articles.body: Russian prosecutors have called for an end to the murder case against the Khachaturyan sisters, saying Krestina, Angelina and Maria Khachaturyan acted in self-defense when they killed their father, Mikhail Khachaturyan, in 2018. The state news agency RIA Novosti reported the prosecution's position from Moscow's Basmanny District Court, where on November 18 the court heard a complaint from Maria Khachaturyan's lawyer. The prosecution of the sisters is one of the most high-profile domestic violence cases in modern Russian history: the three sisters said their father had subjected them to years of physical and sexual abuse, and their case became a symbol of the campaign for a domestic violence law in Russia. The investigation into the sisters resumed in 2026 after years of legal limbo, and the prosecutors' call to drop the case is a significant turn. If the court agrees, the sisters will be freed from the threat of a murder conviction after eight years of proceedings. The case has divided Russian society, with supporters seeing the sisters as victims of abuse and critics insisting that killing a parent can never be justified.

articles.title: Russia's FSB has a list of at least 1,000 Azov personnel who could face prosecution, Mediazona reports
articles.description: Russia's Federal Security Service has a roster naming at least 1,084 people connected to the Azov brigade who could face prosecution in Russia, the independent outlet Mediazona has learned. The list includes people who held civilian jobs with the brigade and still live in Russian-occupied territory.
articles.body: Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) has a roster of Azov personnel that names at least 1,084 people who could face prosecution in Russia, the independent outlet Mediazona has learned, as reported by Meduza. The list includes people who held civilian jobs with the Ukrainian brigade and still live in Russian-occupied territory, not only fighters. The roster has already been presented at least twice in the Southern District Military Court in Rostov-on-Don, including during the trial of Viktoria Tinkova, who was charged with participating in a terrorist group and on November 18 was sentenced to five years in a minimum-security penal colony. Mediazona's reporters believe the roster may also be used in other cases involving charges of participating in a terrorist group. Russian authorities have designated Azov and Aidar as terrorist organizations, and Mediazona has published an in-depth report on such convictions. The existence of a list of more than a thousand names suggests the prosecutions could extend far beyond the soldiers captured at Azovstal, reaching civilians who worked for the brigade in any capacity.

articles.title: Russia has closed one in six maternity hospitals in six years, BBC Russia finds
articles.description: Russia has closed one in six of its maternity hospitals in the past six years, BBC Russia has found, as officials blame falling birth rates and declining women's health. The closures come as the Kremlin pushes Russians to have more children and surveys them about their family plans every three years.
articles.body: Russia has closed one in six of its maternity hospitals in the past six years, BBC Russia has found, according to Meduza's English edition. Officials blame the closures on falling birth rates and declining women's health, but the scale of the shutdowns underlines how the country's demographic crisis is reshaping its healthcare system. The findings were published on the same day Meduza reported that Rosstat, Russia's statistics agency, will survey Russians about their plans to have children every three years instead of every five, after President Vladimir Putin ordered the agency in February 2026 to shorten the interval. The Economic Development Ministry has already drafted a resolution implementing the change, set to take effect in 2027. The contradiction is stark: the state is intensifying its monitoring of Russians' reproductive plans while the infrastructure for giving birth safely is shrinking. Russia's birth rate has fallen to historic lows, and the war has accelerated the decline, with hundreds of thousands of men killed, wounded or abroad. The maternity hospital closures are concentrated in smaller towns, leaving women in rural areas further from care.

articles.title: Russians to be asked about their plans to have children every three years
articles.description: Rosstat will survey Russians about their plans to have children every three years instead of every five, after President Vladimir Putin ordered the agency in February 2026 to shorten the interval between surveys. The Economic Development Ministry has already drafted a resolution implementing the change, set to take effect in 2027.
articles.body: Rosstat, Russia's federal statistics agency, will survey Russians about their plans to have children every three years instead of every five, after President Vladimir Putin ordered the agency in February 2026 to shorten the interval between surveys. The Economic Development Ministry has already drafted a resolution implementing the change, which is set to take effect in 2027. The move reflects the Kremlin's deepening anxiety about Russia's demographic decline: the birth rate has fallen to historic lows, and the war in Ukraine has accelerated the trend, with hundreds of thousands of men killed, wounded or living abroad. The more frequent surveys will give the government a closer read on whether its pro-natalist policies — including cash payments for mothers and restrictions on abortion — are changing behaviour. Critics note that the state is intensifying its surveillance of private reproductive decisions while the infrastructure for childbirth shrinks: BBC Russia found this week that one in six maternity hospitals has closed in the past six years. The survey change is a small administrative step, but it captures how demographic policy has become a central preoccupation of the Russian state.

articles.title: Russian businessman sentenced to 23 years in prison over killing of General Yaroslav Moskalik
articles.description: A Russian businessman has been sentenced to 23 years in prison over the killing of General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior Russian military officer. The case is one of several high-profile assassinations of Russian generals during the war.
articles.body: A Russian businessman has been sentenced to 23 years in prison over the killing of General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior Russian military officer, Meduza's English edition reports. The sentencing is one of the longest handed down in a case connected to the assassinations of Russian generals during the war in Ukraine, a series of killings that has exposed the vulnerability of senior officers even far from the front. Moskalik was a deputy chief of the Main Operations Directorate of the Russian General Staff, and his killing was treated in Moscow as a major security failure. The businessman was found guilty of involvement in the attack, and the 23-year sentence reflects how seriously the Russian state treats the targeting of its military leadership. The case is part of a wider pattern: several Russian generals and senior officers have been killed in assassinations attributed to Ukrainian intelligence, and Russian courts have handed down long sentences in the cases that reach trial. The verdict will be closely watched as a signal of how the Kremlin intends to deter further attacks on its commanders.

articles.title: Moscow and Helsinki agree on one thing: Russia never demanded Finland leave NATO
articles.description: Finland has no intention of leaving NATO and will remain a member of the alliance, President Alexander Stubb said, responding to a report in the German tabloid Bild that Russia had demanded Finland leave NATO as part of peace talks on Ukraine. Moscow officially denies making any such demand.
articles.body: Finland has no intention of leaving NATO and will remain a member of the alliance, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in an interview with the newspaper Ilta-Sanomat, responding to a report in the German tabloid Bild that Russia had demanded Finland leave NATO as part of peace talks on Ukraine. Stubb said Finland's NATO membership 'will not be reversed in any form. Finland doesn't want that, and NATO doesn't want that.' Moscow officially denies making any such demand: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, 'I'm not aware of that. No, no one made [that proposal]. It definitely didn't come up.' Finland joined NATO in April 2023, having applied shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the question of whether Moscow would seek to reverse that has hung over the peace diplomacy. In late October, Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke with Putin by phone. The episode shows how the peace talks are generating claims and counter-claims about what is on the table, and how the Nordic states are watching the diplomacy for any sign that their security could be bargained away.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine's battlefield positions are strong; Ukrainian team to meet Trump representatives and European leaders
articles.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday evening that Ukraine's positions on the battlefield are strong, citing the defence of the contested towns of Dobropillia and Kostiantynivka, where Russian forces are making intensive attempts to advance. He also announced that a Ukrainian delegation will meet representatives of Donald Trump and European leaders as diplomacy around the war intensifies ahead of the Shenzhen summit.
articles.body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday evening that Ukraine's positions on the battlefield are strong, citing the defence of two frontline towns in eastern Donetsk region, Dobropillia and Kostiantynivka, against Russian attacks. Speaking in his nightly video address and referring to a report from top commander Mykhailo Drapatyi, Zelenskyy said Russian forces are making 'very intensive attempts' to advance towards both towns, 'and we are destroying the occupiers.' Russia's military has said in recent months that its forces have captured both cities; Ukraine denies they have changed hands. Zelenskyy also announced that a Ukrainian delegation will meet representatives of Donald Trump and European leaders, as the diplomacy around ending the war enters its most active phase in months — a day before Trump, Putin and Xi meet in Shenzhen, where Ukraine is not invited. The comments come as Ukraine's General Staff reported 165 combat engagements in the past day, with Pokrovsk remaining the most active sector, and as Russian strikes continue against energy infrastructure. The president's message was aimed at reassuring Ukrainians and partners that Kyiv's negotiating position is not collapsing on the battlefield even as the great powers talk over its head.

articles.title: Ukraine carried out the Crimean Bridge strike without Starlink, using its own communications technology, officer tells The Times
articles.description: Ukraine carried out its strike on the Crimean Bridge without using Starlink, relying instead on its own communications technology, a Ukrainian officer has told The Times. The strike destroyed the bridge's central road section while the railway reportedly still works, and it came amid a wider campaign against Russian logistics in occupied Crimea.
articles.body: Ukraine carried out its strike on the Crimean Bridge without using Starlink, relying instead on its own communications technology, a Ukrainian officer has told The Times. The detail matters because the operation depended on secure, long-range communications to guide the attack, and it shows Ukraine has built its own alternatives to the satellite system it has relied on for much of the war. The strike destroyed the bridge's central road section, while the railway reportedly still works, and video from a train showed the wrecked span after the attack. The bridge is Russia's only direct land link to occupied Crimea and a key supply route for its forces, and it has been attacked several times since 2022. The revelation comes as the bridge's road section was partially reopened after being closed for about 12 hours, with Russian officials calling the damage 'minor.' Ukraine's defence forces have not commented on the strike itself. The use of domestic communications technology is also a signal to Kyiv's partners that Ukraine is reducing its dependence on systems controlled by private companies.

articles.title: Russian drones hit an apartment block in Chuhuiv, injuring people
articles.description: Russian drones struck an apartment block in Chuhuiv, in the Kharkiv region, injuring residents who had to be rescued from the upper floors. The attack is part of the nightly drone campaign against Ukrainian cities that has continued even as diplomacy around the war intensifies.
articles.body: Russian drones hit an apartment block in Chuhuiv, in the Kharkiv region, injuring residents who had to be rescued from the upper floors after the strike. Emergency services worked through the night to evacuate people from the damaged building, which was hit as part of the nightly drone campaign against Ukrainian cities. The attack came on the same day drone debris fell in Kyiv's Pechersk district, hospitalising one person, and Russian strikes hit energy facilities in the Odesa region, leaving two districts without power. The strikes underline that Russia's campaign against Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure has not paused even as the great powers prepare to meet in Shenzhen to discuss the war. Chuhuiv, near Kharkiv, has been repeatedly targeted throughout the full-scale invasion because of its position close to the Russian border. The attack is a reminder that the war's civilian toll continues to rise daily, even as the diplomatic focus shifts to the summit.

articles.title: Drone debris falls in Kyiv's Pechersk district, one person hospitalized
articles.description: Wreckage from a downed Russian drone fell in Kyiv's Pechersk district on Wednesday, injuring one person who was taken to hospital. The incident came during another night of Russian drone attacks on the capital and other Ukrainian cities.
articles.body: Wreckage from a downed Russian drone fell in Kyiv's Pechersk district on Wednesday, injuring one person who was taken to hospital. Air defences intercepted the drone over the capital, but falling debris caused injuries and damage in the central district, one of the most densely built-up areas of the city. The incident came during another night of Russian drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, which also saw a strike on an apartment block in Chuhuiv and attacks on energy facilities in the Odesa region. The capital has been under near-nightly attack for weeks, and the falling-debris injuries are a regular feature of the campaign, even when air defences work as intended. Ukrainian officials have repeatedly said the country needs more interceptor missiles to protect its cities, and air defence remains Kyiv's top request to its partners. The Pechersk incident is a small-scale reminder of the daily danger facing Kyiv's residents, even on days when the diplomatic news dominates the headlines.

articles.title: Attack on energy facilities in Odesa region leaves two districts without power
articles.description: Russian strikes on energy facilities in the Odesa region have left two districts without power, Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday. The attacks are part of the sustained campaign against Ukraine's power grid as winter approaches.
articles.body: Russian strikes on energy facilities in the Odesa region have left two districts without power, Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday. The attacks hit the region's energy infrastructure as part of the sustained campaign against Ukraine's power grid, which has intensified as winter approaches. The outages come a day after President Zelenskyy warned that Russia is preparing a new missile strike, and as evening strikes have repeatedly knocked out power in cities including Dnipro, which has now suffered six blackouts in two weeks. The Odesa region, on the Black Sea coast, is a key hub for Ukraine's grain exports and a frequent target of Russian attacks on port and energy infrastructure. Repair crews are working to restore supply, but officials warn that the damage to the grid is cumulative, and each new strike makes the system harder to keep running through the winter. The attacks underline why air-defence supplies remain Kyiv's most urgent request to its partners, and why the EU's proposed €45 billion loan for Ukraine in 2027 is framed around keeping the country running.

articles.title: Journalist Khrystyna Lysenko killed during shelling of Odesa
articles.description: Journalist Khrystyna Lysenko was killed during shelling of Odesa on Wednesday, Ukrainska Pravda reports. She was on her way to work when the attack hit, and her death is the latest in the toll of media workers killed in the war.
articles.body: Journalist Khrystyna Lysenko was killed during shelling of Odesa on Wednesday, Ukrainska Pravda reports. She was on her way to work when the attack hit the city, and her death is the latest in the toll of media workers killed since the full-scale invasion began. Lysenko's killing comes on a day when Russian strikes also hit energy facilities in the Odesa region, leaving two districts without power, and drone attacks struck Chuhuiv and Kyiv. Odesa, Ukraine's main Black Sea port, has been under regular attack throughout the war, with Russia targeting its port infrastructure, energy grid and residential areas. The death of a journalist on her way to work is a reminder that the war's civilian toll is not limited to the front line: reporters, medics, rescue workers and ordinary commuters are among those killed in strikes on cities far from the fighting. Ukrainian media organisations have recorded dozens of journalists killed since February 2022, and Lysenko's name will be added to that list.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones nearly halved Russian oil refining in 20 days
articles.description: Sustained Ukrainian drone strikes have nearly halved Russia's oil refining capacity in just 20 days, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The campaign against refineries is one of Ukraine's most effective long-range operations, cutting into the fuel supplies that fund and power Russia's war.
articles.body: Sustained Ukrainian drone strikes have nearly halved Russia's oil refining capacity in just 20 days, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The campaign against refineries is one of Ukraine's most effective long-range operations: by hitting the plants that turn crude oil into fuel, Kyiv is cutting into both the domestic fuel supply and the export revenues that fund Russia's war. The latest strikes hit two refineries in the Krasnodar region — the Afipsky and Ilsky plants — injuring four people and starting fires, in an attack that was already reported in the morning digest. The scale of the refining losses is now showing up in Russian domestic markets: Russia's seaborne gasoline imports hit a record 390,000 tonnes in October, a sign that the country is struggling to meet its own fuel needs. The campaign has also drawn criticism from some in Washington, with a deputy to the US defence secretary condemning Ukraine's deep strikes into Russia as bringing 'pain to the population.' Kyiv argues the refineries are legitimate military targets that sustain Russia's war machine, and the results suggest the strategy is working.

articles.title: Putin plans to fight against Ukraine at least until the end of winter, Western intelligence says
articles.description: Vladimir Putin plans to keep fighting against Ukraine at least until the end of winter, Western intelligence assessments say, meaning Moscow is not expected to stop the war this winter even as the Shenzhen summit approaches. The assessment undercuts hopes that the trilateral meeting will produce a quick ceasefire.
articles.body: Vladimir Putin plans to keep fighting against Ukraine at least until the end of winter, according to Western intelligence assessments reported by Ukrainska Pravda. The assessment means Moscow is not expected to stop the war this winter, even as Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Putin prepare to meet in Shenzhen on Thursday to discuss the conflict. The intelligence view undercuts hopes that the trilateral summit will produce a quick ceasefire, and it fits with the Kremlin's own signals: at a closed seminar for United Russia deputies, Kremlin officials told the party to prepare for 'victory,' and the Dossier Center has reported that the Kremlin is preparing talking points to present any peace deal as a victory. The assessment also fits the pattern on the ground, where Russian forces continue to press in Donetsk region and to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure, while Ukraine hits Russian refineries and the Crimean Bridge. For Kyiv and its European partners, the message is that the war will continue through the winter regardless of what is said in Shenzhen, and that air defence and energy supplies remain the most urgent needs.

articles.title: GTA VI reviews land: 99 on Metacritic, tying Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game ever
articles.description: The review embargo for Grand Theft Auto VI lifted on Wednesday morning, and the verdict is historic: the game holds a 99 on Metacritic from 132 critic reviews, tying The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (1998) as the highest-rated game in the site's history. IGN gave it 10/10, calling it 'the single most impressive video game I have ever played.' The game unlocks at midnight local time on Thursday, November 19.
articles.body: The review embargo for Grand Theft Auto VI lifted at 6:00 AM ET on Wednesday, November 18, and the first wave of reviews is historic: the game holds a 99 Metascore on PlayStation 5 from 132 critic reviews, tying Nintendo's 1998 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as the highest-rated game in Metacritic's history, with 109 of the 132 scored reviews awarding perfect 100s and the lowest score so far a 90. IGN gave it 10/10, with critic Luke Reilly calling it 'the single most impressive video game I have ever played,' while GameSpot, Eurogamer, The Guardian, VGC, Game Informer and The Washington Post all awarded full marks; OpenCritic shows a 99 Top Critic Average with 100% of critics recommending it. Reviewers praised the open world, the story and the relationship between protagonists Jason and Lucia, with some noting clunky combat controls and late-game pacing issues. The game rolls out worldwide at midnight local time on November 19, starting in New Zealand, and Take-Two shares rose more than 8% in early trading on the review news. Sensor Tower estimates about 17 million copies already sold for more than $1.65 billion before launch. The standard edition costs $79.99 and the Ultimate Edition $99.99.

articles.title: GTA VI launch eve: midnight unlocks, a PS5 update to install first, and a 24-hour YouTube stream
articles.description: Grand Theft Auto VI unlocks at midnight local time on Thursday, November 19, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, with New Zealand going first. PlayStation says a PS5 system software update is required before playing, and YouTube is running a 24-hour launch stream with 31 creators from around the world.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI unlocks at midnight local time on Thursday, November 19, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, with New Zealand going first — midnight there is 11:00 AM GMT on Wednesday, November 18 — and the rest of the world following the clock through the day. Millions of players have already pre-loaded the game, and Rockstar has confirmed the launch is midnight local time in every region. There is admin to do before the unlock: PlayStation says a PS5 system software update is required before you can play, and its support account told players on November 18 to download it before midnight on November 19. Microsoft's Xbox Wire posted a 'How to Get Ready for November 19' checklist on November 17. YouTube is running a 24-hour launch stream starting at 11 PM ET on Wednesday with a warm-up, followed by the main stream at midnight in New York, with 31 creators from around the world taking part. The game has already been nominated for Game of the Year at The Game Awards, where it leads with eight nominations. For players who want to avoid spoilers, the advice is simple: New Zealand players get the game 13 hours before the UK and 18 hours before New York, so spoilers will be everywhere before most people can play.

articles.title: Rare cuts the Sea of Thieves client by 50% — freeing up SSD space the day GTA VI launches
articles.description: Rare has announced a major update for Sea of Thieves, out on November 19, that cuts the game's client size by about 50% on all platforms — down to 53.2 GB on Steam and just 28.3 GB on Xbox One. The studio says it removed years of accumulated unused files from the long-running live-service game.
articles.body: Rare has announced a major update for Sea of Thieves, out on November 19, that cuts the game's client size by about 50% on all platforms. The studio says it reviewed the game's resources and removed years of accumulated unused files, addressing one of the key problems facing long-running live-service games: the client swelling with every content update. After the update, the game will weigh 53.2 GB on Steam and just 28.3 GB on Xbox One. The timing is pointed: the update lands on the same day as the global release of GTA VI, which has prompted companies like EA to publicly beg players on social media not to delete their games to make room for Rockstar's blockbuster. Rare's move is the opposite approach — making room for its own players instead. The update is also a reminder of how the industry is adapting to the storage crunch: with games routinely topping 100 GB, a 50% cut is a meaningful quality-of-life improvement for players on consoles with limited SSD space. Rare recently moved under the wing of Activision Blizzard, and the Sea of Thieves update is one of its first major moves under the new structure.

articles.title: Publishers cleared the calendar around GTA VI: Fable slips to February 2027, Squadron 42 to mid-2027
articles.description: The 'GTA effect' has reshaped the release calendar: with almost no major games launching in November besides GTA VI, several publishers moved their titles away from Rockstar's launch window. Fable now arrives on February 23, 2027, Squadron 42 in the second quarter of 2027, and Danganronpa 2x2 on January 14, 2027.
articles.body: The 'GTA effect' has reshaped the release calendar around Grand Theft Auto VI: after the summer, the November schedule was noticeably reworked, and apart from GTA VI almost no major games are launching in the month. Several publishers openly moved their titles away from Rockstar's launch window. Playground Games' Fable will now arrive on February 23, 2027, Cloud Imperium Games' Squadron 42 has slipped to the second quarter of 2027, and Spike Chunsoft's Danganronpa 2x2 comes out on January 14, 2027. The games that did stay in November are mostly smaller releases: Nintendo's remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Switch 2 and World of Warcraft: Forever arrived on November 5, a Shrek 2 remaster and Warhammer Survivors on November 10, and the Russian indie Toto's Journey — a dog adventure inspired by The Wizard of Oz — launches on November 18, the day before GTA VI. The pattern shows how completely one game can dominate the industry's planning: publishers would rather delay by months than compete with the most anticipated release in years.

articles.title: Toto's Journey launches today — a Russian indie dog adventure inspired by The Wizard of Oz
articles.description: Toto's Journey, a Russian indie adventure starring a dog named Toto in a fairy-tale world inspired by The Wizard of Oz and The Wizard of the Emerald City, launches on Steam on Wednesday, November 18 — the day before GTA VI. Reviewers have already compared it to Stray, the cat adventure that became a hit in 2022.
articles.body: Toto's Journey, a Russian indie adventure game starring a dog named Toto in a fairy-tale world inspired by L. Frank Baum's The Wonderful Wizard of Oz and Alexander Volkov's The Wizard of the Emerald City, launches on Steam on Wednesday, November 18 — the day before GTA VI. The game has already drawn comparisons to Stray, the 2022 cat adventure that became a surprise hit, with players guiding a small animal through a strange and beautiful world. Launching the day before the biggest game release in history is a bold choice, but the developers are betting that players looking for something gentle and whimsical will find it while the rest of the industry is focused on Vice City. The game is one of the few notable November releases that did not move away from GTA VI's launch window, alongside the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and World of Warcraft: Forever earlier in the month. For players who want a quieter alternative to Rockstar's blockbuster, Toto's Journey is the most charming option on the calendar.

articles.title: Trump lands in Shenzhen as Xi gives him an 'unprecedented' airport greeting ahead of the three-way summit
articles.description: President Donald Trump arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday, where Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted him at the airport — a gesture CNN describes as unprecedented. Trump will meet Xi and Vladimir Putin on Thursday in the first-ever in-person three-way summit of the three leaders, with nuclear weapons, Iran and Ukraine expected on the agenda. Putin arrived the same day, and Xi met him separately, calling Russia-China ties 'firm as a mountain.'
articles.body: President Donald Trump arrived in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, November 18, where Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted him at the airport — a gesture CNN describes as unprecedented for a visiting leader. Trump is in China for the APEC summit and will meet Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, November 19, in the first-ever in-person three-way summit of the leaders of China, the United States and Russia. Putin arrived in Shenzhen the same day and met Xi separately, with Xi saying relations between Russia and China 'stand as firm as a mountain amid wind and rain.' The White House says the trilateral talks will focus on nuclear weapons rather than the war in Ukraine, though Trump has also said he wants to discuss the Ukraine settlement with both leaders, and he plans a separate bilateral meeting with Putin. The Financial Times reports the meeting will have no pre-agreed agenda, and Trump does not expect to reach an agreement on nuclear arms — he wants only to start a discussion between the world's three largest nuclear powers. The summit has already been dubbed a 'New Yalta' in the media, and Kyiv and its European partners are watching closely for any deal struck over Ukraine's head. CNN's analysis notes the symbolism is stark: three great powers sending a signal of dominance that deliberately excludes smaller nations, with breakthroughs not expected.

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO could be the largest stock market debut of all time — worth as much as $1.4 trillion
articles.description: Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be worth as much as $1.4 trillion in a public listing that would be the largest stock market debut of all time, CNN reports. Founded just five years ago, the company has become one of the central players in the AI race, and an IPO of that size would dwarf previous record listings.
articles.body: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, could be worth as much as $1.4 trillion in a public listing that would be the largest stock market debut of all time, CNN reports. Founded just five years ago, Anthropic has become one of the central players in the AI race, competing with OpenAI and Google while building a reputation for safety-focused development. A valuation of $1.4 trillion would dwarf previous record IPOs and would place the company among the most valuable in the world on day one. The report comes in a week when AI companies dominate business news, from chip export controls to the Suno music lawsuits, and it reflects how completely investor enthusiasm for AI has reshaped the market. For the wider tech industry, an Anthropic listing of this scale would test whether public markets are ready to price AI companies at levels previously reserved for the largest incumbents. No timing for the offering has been confirmed, and the figure is a potential valuation rather than a filed price range.

articles.title: Mary Peltola ousts incumbent Dan Sullivan in Alaska Senate race, giving Democrats 56 seats
articles.description: Mary Peltola has ousted incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska's Senate race, CNN projects, in a Democratic pickup that gives the party 56 seats in the Senate. The result caps a strong election cycle for Democrats, who also saw Hakeem Jeffries win the House speaker nomination overwhelmingly this week.
articles.body: Mary Peltola has ousted incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan in Alaska's Senate race, CNN projects, in a Democratic pickup that gives the party 56 seats in the Senate. The result is one of the most significant of the election cycle: Sullivan was a two-term incumbent in a state that has long leaned Republican, and Peltola's victory extends the Democrats' Senate majority to a commanding margin. The win caps a strong cycle for the party, which also saw Hakeem Jeffries win the Democratic nomination for House speaker overwhelmingly this week, putting him on course to become the first Black speaker when the new Congress convenes in January. The Alaska result will shape the balance of power in Washington as the new Congress takes up the agenda for 2027, including the future of Ukraine aid, which NBC News reports Republicans in Congress are using as leverage against Democrats. For Republicans, the loss of a seat they had held for more than a decade is a setback that will prompt questions about the party's direction after the midterms.

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries overwhelmingly wins House speaker nomination, on course to become the first Black speaker
articles.description: Hakeem Jeffries has overwhelmingly won the Democratic nomination for speaker of the House, CNN reports, despite threats from ultra-progressives. He is all but certain to lead the House from January, when he would become the first Black speaker in American history.
articles.body: Hakeem Jeffries has overwhelmingly won the Democratic nomination for speaker of the House, CNN reports, despite threats from ultra-progressives to challenge his leadership. He is all but certain to lead the House when the new Congress convenes in January, when he would become the first Black speaker in American history. The nomination caps a strong election cycle for the Democrats, who also picked up a Senate seat in Alaska, where Mary Peltola ousted incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan to give the party 56 seats. Jeffries, who has led House Democrats since 2023, faced pressure from the party's left flank, but the size of his victory suggests the caucus is united behind him as it prepares to take power. The new Congress will take up a crowded agenda in 2027, including the future of Ukraine aid and the sweeping investigations into the Trump administration that Democrats have been laying the groundwork for. Jeffries' elevation is a historic milestone for the House and for American politics, and it sets the terms for the relationship between the Democratic-controlled Congress and the White House.

articles.title: What's causing all these outages? The internet is 'held together with shoestring and bubblegum,' CNN analysis says
articles.description: After a week of disruptive tech failures — bank outages, a Microsoft disruption, an FAA ground stop and a classified NSA network going down — CNN asks what is actually causing the cascade. The analysis argues the internet's infrastructure is fragile, held together with 'shoestring and bubblegum,' and that the failures are connected by shared dependencies rather than coincidence.
articles.body: After a week of disruptive technology failures, CNN asks what is actually causing the cascade of outages. The list is long: major US banks including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo suffered online banking outages on Monday; Microsoft had a major service disruption on Friday; the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop and paused Juniper router installations; and a classified NSA internal communications network went down. The Trump administration has dismissed fears of a crisis, but CNN's analysis argues the failures expose how fragile the internet's underlying infrastructure really is — 'held together with shoestring and bubblegum,' in the words of one expert. The outages are connected not by a single cause but by shared dependencies: a handful of cloud providers, a small number of router and software vendors, and a web of services that all depend on each other. When one piece fails, the effects cascade across banks, airlines, government networks and everyday services. The analysis is a follow-up to the morning digest's story on what should scare Americans about the outage blitz, and it reaches a similar conclusion: the systems that run modern life are more brittle than most people assume, and the week of failures is a warning rather than a coincidence.

articles.title: Intense flooding slams Florida from a developing storm that could snarl early Thanksgiving travel
articles.description: Intense flooding has slammed coastal Florida, with more than a foot of rain soaking parts of the state from a developing storm that could snarl early Thanksgiving travel on the East Coast. The storm arrives just as millions of Americans begin travelling for the holiday.
articles.body: Intense flooding has slammed coastal Florida, with more than a foot of rain soaking parts of the state from a developing storm that could snarl early Thanksgiving travel on the East Coast. The storm system is gathering strength off the Florida coast and is expected to move north, bringing heavy rain and the risk of flooding to the Eastern Seaboard in the days before Thanksgiving. The timing is the worst possible: millions of Americans are about to begin travelling for the holiday, one of the busiest travel periods of the year, and the storm threatens to disrupt flights and road travel across the region. Florida's coastal communities are already dealing with flooded streets and waterlogged homes, and forecasters warn the rain will continue. The storm is a reminder of how the holiday travel season is increasingly vulnerable to extreme weather, and it follows a year of disruptive storms across the southeastern United States. Travellers are being advised to check conditions before setting out, with the worst of the weather expected to arrive as the holiday exodus peaks.

articles.title: Russian military transport aircraft crashes in Siberia, killing all 19 aboard, defence ministry says
articles.description: A Russian military transport aircraft has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people aboard, the defence ministry says. The crash, in the Kemerovo region, is the same incident reported on Tuesday evening, with the death toll now confirmed at 19.
articles.body: A Russian military transport aircraft has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people aboard, the Russian defence ministry says. The crash happened in the Kemerovo region, and the death toll of 19 is now confirmed — an update to the report carried on Tuesday evening, which said the plane had crashed and all crew members were reportedly killed without giving a figure. The aircraft was a military transport plane, and the ministry said all 19 people on board died in the crash. The cause of the accident has not been disclosed, and Russian officials have not said what the aircraft was carrying or where it was headed. The crash is one of the deadliest Russian military aviation accidents of the war, and it comes as the Russian air force has been stretched by more than four years of operations in Ukraine. Military transport crashes in Russia are not uncommon — ageing aircraft, heavy use and maintenance pressures have all been cited in past accidents — but the loss of 19 people in a single incident is a significant blow. The defence ministry's confirmation of the toll closes the uncertainty around the incident, though questions about its cause remain.

articles.title: Israel's parliament elects a new Knesset speaker, weakening Netanyahu's grip on power
articles.description: Israel's parliament has elected a new Knesset speaker, in a move that weakens Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's grip on power. The election gives the opposition Yashar party greater control over the legislative agenda.
articles.body: Israel's parliament has elected a new Knesset speaker, in a move that weakens Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's grip on power. The election gives the opposition Yashar party greater control over the legislative agenda, a significant shift in the balance of power inside the Israeli parliament. The speaker of the Knesset controls the flow of legislation, sets the parliamentary timetable and can shape which bills reach a vote, so the change of hands is more than symbolic. For Netanyahu, who has held power through a series of fragile coalitions, the loss of the speakership is a setback that could complicate his legislative programme. The move comes amid ongoing political turbulence in Israel, where the government has faced pressure over the war in Gaza, the hostage issue and the economy. The opposition's gain of the speaker's chair gives it a new lever over the government's agenda, and it could make it harder for Netanyahu to push through controversial legislation in the months ahead.

articles.title: TikTok says 94% of songs that entered the Billboard Global 200 in 2025 went viral on its platform first
articles.description: TikTok's 2026 Music Impact Report, prepared by Luminate and published on Wednesday, says 94% of the songs that entered the Billboard Global 200 in 2025 went viral on TikTok first — up from 84% in 2024. The finding underlines how completely the short-video platform now controls the pipeline for breaking new music worldwide.
articles.body: TikTok says 94% of the songs that entered the Billboard Global 200 in 2025 went viral on TikTok first, according to the platform's 2026 Music Impact Report, prepared by Luminate and published on Wednesday, November 18. That figure is up from 84% in 2024, showing TikTok's grip on music discovery tightening further even as the platform faces regulatory pressure in the United States. The report measures how songs move from TikTok virality into the chart compiled from streaming data in more than 200 countries and regions, and the near-total share suggests that for a new song to break globally, a TikTok moment is now close to a precondition rather than a bonus. For labels and artists, the finding sharpens the strategic question of how much of a release campaign should be built around the platform, and for the wider industry it reinforces TikTok's position as the most powerful discovery engine in music. The report lands as TikTok's role in the music business keeps expanding from promotion into distribution, with the company positioning itself as a route to stardom for unsigned artists.

articles.title: HYBE makes $79M bid for controlling stake in Japan's KeyHolder, which has interests in SKE48 and Nogizaka46
articles.description: HYBE has made a $79 million bid for a controlling stake in KeyHolder, the Japanese company with interests in idol groups SKE48 and Nogizaka46. Agreements with KeyHolder's largest shareholders, including J Trust, already cover the bid's minimum threshold.
articles.body: HYBE has made a $79 million bid for a controlling stake in KeyHolder, the Japanese company with interests in idol groups SKE48 and Nogizaka46, Music Business Worldwide reports. Agreements with KeyHolder's largest shareholders, including J Trust, already cover the bid's minimum threshold, suggesting the deal is likely to go through. The move is HYBE's latest step in its expansion into Japan, the world's second-largest music market, where the Korean entertainment giant has been building a local presence through acquisitions and partnerships. KeyHolder's interests in SKE48 and Nogizaka46 — two of Japan's most established idol groups — would give HYBE a foothold in the Japanese idol business, a market with a very different structure from the K-pop system HYBE dominates at home. The bid comes as HYBE continues to diversify beyond its core K-pop business, following its investments in Latin music, gaming and technology. For the Japanese idol industry, the arrival of a Korean giant as a controlling shareholder is a significant moment, and it could accelerate the convergence of the J-pop and K-pop systems.

articles.title: Ignacio Meyer appointed President of Universal Music Latin America & Iberian Peninsula
articles.description: Ignacio Meyer has been appointed President of Universal Music Latin America & Iberian Peninsula, Universal Music Group announced on Wednesday. Meyer will report to Felipe Holguín, who was named CEO of the division on Tuesday.
articles.body: Ignacio Meyer has been appointed President of Universal Music Latin America & Iberian Peninsula, Universal Music Group announced on Wednesday, November 18. Meyer will report to Felipe Holguín, who was named CEO of the division on Tuesday, completing a new leadership team for one of UMG's most important growth regions. Latin music has been one of the fastest-growing segments of the global recorded music market for several years, driven by streaming and by the global crossover of Latin artists. Meyer's appointment is part of a wider reshaping of UMG's Latin American operations, which also saw Holguín take the top job this week. The division covers Latin America and the Iberian Peninsula — Spain and Portugal — and its leadership will be responsible for one of the most competitive markets in the industry, where UMG competes with Sony and Warner for the biggest Latin stars. The appointments come as the Latin music business continues to expand beyond its traditional markets, with artists from the region now regularly topping global charts.

articles.title: Notes.fm partners with Musixmatch to bring time-synced lyrics to its distribution platform for independent artists
articles.description: Notes.fm, the music royalty collection and distribution platform from Stem co-founder Tim Luckow, has partnered with Musixmatch to bring time-synced lyrics to its distribution platform for independent artists. The deal gives indie artists access to a feature usually reserved for major-label releases.
articles.body: Notes.fm has partnered with Musixmatch to bring time-synced lyrics to its distribution platform for independent artists, Music Business Worldwide reports. Notes.fm is a music royalty collection and distribution platform from Tim Luckow, the co-founder of Stem, and the Musixmatch deal gives its users access to the time-synced lyrics that appear on streaming services alongside the music. For independent artists, the feature is a meaningful upgrade: synced lyrics are a standard part of the listening experience on Spotify, Apple Music and other services, but getting them set up has traditionally required going through a major distributor or label. The partnership is part of a wider trend of distribution platforms adding services that were once the preserve of labels, from royalty collection to marketing tools. Musixmatch, which supplies lyrics to the major streaming services, gains access to a growing pool of independent artists, while Notes.fm strengthens its pitch to artists who want label-grade infrastructure without signing a label deal. The deal is a small one in the scheme of the music business, but it is a useful sign of how the independent sector keeps closing the gap with the majors.

articles.title: Beyoncé becomes the first artist ever to earn 100 Grammy nominations
articles.description: Beyoncé has made history as the first artist ever to earn 100 Grammy Award nominations, with the 2027 nominations announced this week. The milestone extends a record she already holds as the most decorated artist in Grammy history, and it comes in a nominations round that also blanked Harry Styles despite an acclaimed 2026 album and a previous Album of the Year win.
articles.body: Beyoncé has made history as the first artist ever to earn 100 Grammy Award nominations, Rolling Stone reports, with the 2027 Grammy nominations announced this week. The milestone extends a record she already holds as the most decorated artist in Grammy history, and it underlines a career that has now spanned more than two decades of Grammy recognition across R&B, pop, country and now the album categories. The nominations round produced several other talking points: Miley Cyrus earned a nod alongside her godmother Dolly Parton, Shakira and Drake drew attention in the Latin categories, and BTS were not nominated despite a major year. The biggest surprise was Harry Styles, whose acclaimed 2026 album and previous Album of the Year win did not translate into a single nomination. The 2027 Grammy Awards ceremony is scheduled for February, and Beyoncé's century of nominations is likely to dominate the build-up. For an artist who has already rewritten the Grammy record books, the 100th nomination is less a surprise than a confirmation of her standing with the Recording Academy.

articles.title: Draco Rosa to receive the 2026 Rolling Stone en Español Legend Award
articles.description: Draco Rosa will be honoured as the 2026 Rolling Stone en Español Legend at the ZYN Rolling Stone en Español Awards, which take place on November 25 and 26 at the Four Seasons Hotel in Mexico City. The award celebrates artists whose careers and influence have left a mark on the history of music in Spanish.
articles.body: Draco Rosa will receive the 2026 Rolling Stone en Español Legend Award, the organisers announced on Wednesday, November 18. The award is a distinction that celebrates artists whose careers, creative vision and influence have left a significant mark on the history of music in Spanish, and Rosa is one of the most decorated figures in Latin music. The ZYN Rolling Stone en Español Awards will take place on November 25 and 26 at the Four Seasons Hotel in Mexico City, bringing together some of the most prominent figures in Spanish-language music and culture. The event is private and tickets will not be available for public sale. Rosa, a Puerto Rican singer-songwriter and producer, has had a career spanning decades, from his early work with Menudo to his solo career and his work as a songwriter and producer for other artists. The Legend Award places him in the company of the most respected names in Latin music, and the Mexico City ceremony will be one of the highlights of the Latin music calendar this year.

articles.title: Lawsuit accusing Selena Gomez and Wondermind co-founders of fraud is dismissed
articles.description: A lawsuit accusing Selena Gomez and the co-founders of her mental health company Wondermind of fraud has been dismissed, Rolling Stone reports. The case had alleged misconduct in the running of the company, which Gomez co-founded to promote mental health awareness.
articles.body: A lawsuit accusing Selena Gomez and the co-founders of her mental health company Wondermind of fraud has been dismissed, Rolling Stone reports. The case had alleged misconduct in the running of Wondermind, the mental health company Gomez co-founded to promote mental health awareness and to provide resources for people struggling with anxiety and depression. The dismissal is a win for Gomez, who has been one of the most prominent celebrity advocates for mental health, and for the company, which has faced scrutiny over its finances and management. The lawsuit's dismissal does not end the wider debate about celebrity-backed wellness companies and the standards they should be held to, but it removes a legal cloud that had hung over Wondermind for months. Gomez has built a business empire that spans music, acting, beauty and mental health, and the Wondermind case was one of the few legal challenges to that empire. The dismissal will allow the company to move on, though the details of the ruling have not been fully disclosed.

articles.title: Stephen Wilson Jr. announces double album and unveils 'I'm a Song' with Chris Stapleton
articles.description: Stephen Wilson Jr. has announced a double album and unveiled its first single, 'I'm a Song,' a collaboration with Chris Stapleton. The announcement is the latest in a run of high-profile country releases this year, and the Stapleton collaboration gives the project immediate star power.
articles.body: Stephen Wilson Jr. has announced a double album and unveiled its first single, 'I'm a Song,' a collaboration with Chris Stapleton, Rolling Stone reports. The announcement is the latest in a run of high-profile country releases this year, and the Stapleton collaboration gives the project immediate star power: Stapleton is one of the most respected voices in modern country, and his presence on the lead single signals the scale of Wilson's ambitions. The double album format is a statement in itself, suggesting an artist with more to say than a single disc can hold. Wilson, who has built a following with his blend of country, rock and Americana, is positioning the album as a major step up from his earlier work. The announcement comes as country music continues its commercial hot streak, with Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' setting the all-time Hot 100 record with 28 weeks at No. 1. For Wilson, the double album and the Stapleton collaboration are a bid to join the top tier of the genre, and the first single will be closely watched as a sign of what the full project holds.

articles.title: Miley Cyrus shares a sweet memory of godmother Dolly Parton as they earn a Grammy nod together
articles.description: Miley Cyrus has shared a sweet memory of her godmother Dolly Parton as the two earned a Grammy nomination together in the 2027 nominations. The nod is a family affair: Parton has been a mentor to Cyrus since childhood, and the joint nomination is a rare moment of shared recognition.
articles.body: Miley Cyrus has shared a sweet memory of her godmother Dolly Parton as the two earned a Grammy nomination together in the 2027 nominations, Rolling Stone reports. The nod is a family affair: Parton has been a mentor to Cyrus since childhood, and the joint nomination is a rare moment of shared recognition for two of the most famous voices in American music. Cyrus spoke warmly about Parton's influence on her career, from her early days as a child star to her reinvention as an adult artist, and the nomination is a reminder of how deeply their careers are intertwined. The 2027 Grammy nominations have produced several family stories — Beyoncé's historic 100th nomination, Harry Styles' surprise blanking — and the Cyrus-Parton nod is one of the most heartwarming. Parton, who has been nominated for Grammys across six decades, remains one of the most beloved figures in music, and the joint nomination with her goddaughter is a fitting addition to her record. The ceremony is scheduled for February, and the pair's nomination will be one of the most closely watched of the night.

articles.title: The Grammy nominations blanked Harry Styles. What happened?
articles.description: Despite an acclaimed 2026 album — and a previous Album of the Year win — Harry Styles was not nominated for a single 2027 Grammy, Rolling Stone reports. The snub is one of the biggest surprises of the nominations round, which also saw Beyoncé make history with her 100th nomination.
articles.body: Despite an acclaimed 2026 album — and a previous Album of the Year win — Harry Styles was not nominated for a single 2027 Grammy, Rolling Stone reports. The snub is one of the biggest surprises of the nominations round, which also saw Beyoncé make history as the first artist to earn 100 nominations and Miley Cyrus earn a nod alongside her godmother Dolly Parton. Styles' 2026 album was widely praised by critics and performed strongly on the charts, and his previous Album of the Year win had seemed to confirm his standing with the Recording Academy. The blanking has prompted questions about what changed: whether the Academy's tastes have shifted, whether the album's campaign fell short, or whether the competition was simply too strong in a year packed with major releases. The snub is also a reminder of how unpredictable the Grammys can be — an artist can go from the top of the podium to off the ballot in a single cycle. For Styles, who has built one of the most successful solo careers of his generation, the omission is unlikely to dent his commercial standing, but it will be one of the most discussed stories of the nominations round.

articles.title: Shakira goes global, Drake gets love: Latin takeaways from the 2027 Grammy nominations
